speechtext:
My right hon. friend is squirming badly now. I was not referring to the words in Hansard, I was referring to his present interpretation. The House is accustomed to the habit of the right hon. gentleman of trying to leave one impression by the use of certain words which are susceptible of a different interpretation. However, that is not an important point. The main thing, is it not, is the fact, as my hon. friend from Brantford will I think agree, that the government has endeavoured to meet the implement manufacturers as we said we would.
We have been able, in a large part at least, and I believe time will show, wholly, to make good to the manufacturers of implements in one way or another whatever they may have lost through tariff reductions. That is only carrying out the policy announced by the Liberal party; for wherever mention is made of reducing the duties on implements of production there is also indicated an intention of reducing the duties on raw materials that enter into the making of the finished product. We have endeavoured as far as possible to meet the manufacturers in that way. A statement has been- quoted from the Massey-Harris Company, and I shall not refer to it again except to say that, interpreted in the way I think it ought to be interpreted, it implies that the government has dealt fairly by that industry and that the company hope, as a result of the changes which have been made, to be in a position to offer their implements cheaper to the farmers and thus do a greater business in the future than they have been able to do in the past. Let me say to my friend the hon. member for Brantford, I have not forgotten my promise, I have fulfilled it.
I have in my hand, from the Brantford Expositor, a series of interviews which I shall not attempt to quote even in part. These interviews are given by the Verity Plow Company, the Cockshutt Plow Company and the Adams Plow Company. The headline reads:
New schedules introduced will constitute some help in matter of lower tariff .... Comments of Brantford implement makers to whom free raw material list had not been previously extended-an undoubted feeling exists of improvement in the outlook-firms will continue to carry on to the best of their ability.
They feel that a very considerable concession has been made and they hope to go on with their business as in the past.
My right hon. friend said this afternoon that the tariff changes had been restricted in their application so as not to touch the constituency of any member of the government in which there might be an implement industry. At any rate, that was the purport of his words. The implication was that, as the common saying is, care had been taken by the government to look after their own relations

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
but that they had let their neighbours' relations shift for themselves. Well, in the constituency, North York, which I have the honour to represent in this parliament there is an important implement industry and one of long standing in this country. I refer to J. Fleury's Sons of Aurora, Ontario, makers of cultivating implements and stock raisers' machines. I need not tell members of the Progressive party who J. Fleury's Sons are in the implement-making business, but I will read a letter which I have received from Mr. Fleury, the head of this firm, so that the House may see what his view is with respect to the changes that have been made. The letter is dated May 1, 1924 at Aurora, Ontario, and it is as follows:
Dear Mr. King:
I wish to express my satisfaction with the amendments put before the House yesterday in connection with duties on materials entering into the cost of implements.
Manufacturers of agricultural implements should feel, I believe, that they have no real grievance; and should be able to show fanners (and no doubt will) that the adjustments of the tariff and the removal of the sales tax will give farmers appreciable benefit in the matter of lower prices.
1 wish to express my appreciation of, and thanks for, your consideration in taking time personally to get a real understanding of the situation of implement manufacturers as affected by the changes in the tariff.
With kind regards, I am,
, Yours faithfully,
H. W. Fleury.
Mr. Fleury, as hon. members are aware, is one of the best known and most important agricultural implement makers in Ontario and indeed in Canada. I may say that when the government decided that the time had come when a change should be made in the. tariff on implements of production we did not try to bring about that change in an indifferent manner or one which would work injury to any industries that could be avoided. We sought to get in touch with the implement makers and I myself asked a number of them and their representatives to come to Ottawa to confer with some of my colleagues and myself. We met them and intimated that in our opinion the interests of Canada demanded that there should be a reduction in the duties on agricultural implements and that the government had made up its mind to that reduction. We added, however, that we wished to make that reduction in such a manner as would do the least possible injury to the industries with which these manufacturers were connected, and we invited suggestions from them as to how, in making the reduction, we could meet them in other ways. We had numerous conferences with them, the result being that we have worked out a 
tariff which in my opinion, not only will prove beneficial to all the basic industries and the manufacturing businesses that develop out of those industries, but which will also prove of advantage to the implement makers themselves. Time will tell, and time I think will prove that the government in this connection has been wise.
I was going to say something on immigration but I shall reserve my remarks on that subject until another occasion, for I fear that other speakers have been much restricted this evening. As we opened- the debate with an exchange of courtesies in the nature of an exchange of editorials from the Farmers' Sun between the leader of the opposition and myself, I think before concluding I should tender him one more from the Farmers' Sun to make up for the "Wobbling Mr. King" one which he sent over to me. My right hon. friend waxed eloquent in his desire for a general election. He said, "We are ready now and we challenge the government to go to the country at once." And all his cohorts alongside him applauded so that it was impossible to hear another sound for a good many seconds. Perhaps the Farmers' Sun is not very far wrong in its view of what my hon. friend's desire is in the matter of a general election. This editorial appears under date April 16 and is headed "Mr. Meighen's hard luck." It reads:
The heaviest cross the Tory politician has to bear is not an overpowering fear of industrial collapse due to tariff reduction. Such a fear might disturb him somewhat, but it could never impress him as a misfortune equal to the circumstance that Hon. Robb's budget should make its appearance a year or more before a general election. It is one thing to plunge into a campaign, broadcasting blue ruin, creating distrust and apprehension by predicting disaster in the future; it is an entirely different proposition to unbalance the judgment of an electorate able to measure of sincerity of election propaganda in the light of experience. By the time the voters of the Dominion are called upon to speak, the changes submitted to the House by the Acting Finance Minister will have had a reasonable trial. It will be known then beyond dispute how much or how little they have benefited agriculture, and the other primary industries of the country. It will be possible, also, to estimate the injury, if any, inflicted upon industries whose protection has been reduced. And this is as it should be.
My right hon. friend says that he is ready for a general election. Let me tell him that this government has not yet finished1 its work of the present parliament. We have a lot more to do; we have only started upon what we hope to be able to do for the country. My right hon. friend may want a general election, but the country does not. The country notes with favour the progress in its affairs that has been made since the present

The Budget-Mr. Crerar
administration has taken office. The people have not failed to observe the improvement in conditions disclosed by each successive budget brought down since the present administration took office. The country is looking to this administration to carry on the good work it has begun and which it intends to continue.
In a word, Mr. Speaker, we believe that in this budget we have been able in very large measure to implement the promises, the professions and the pledges which we made to the electorate in the general election of 1921. We believe that we have established a policy that is entitled to be called a real national policy, because it is so framed as to serve not one class but all classes as well as all interests, manufacturing, commercial, and financial. We want to see that policy given a trial. We believe that if it is given a trial this country will witness a forward progressive movement such as it has not known for many years, and that when the time does come that we appeal to the people again for their support, they will express their confidence in a government which has lived up to its convictions, carried out the promises which it made to the electorate, and conducted the nation's affairs with the interests of the people ever at heart.
Let me say in conclusion that in what we have done not only have we been seeking to improve the country industrially, but we have been seeking also to unite the nation from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We have viewed with a good deal of concern the division which has sprung up between eastern and western Canada. We have felt that it was not good for Canada to be divided into two great sections, each becoming more and more class conscious-the West feeling that it had a grievance against the East, the East bitter in its antagonism towards the West. We have sought therefore a policy which would bring about national unity and demonstrate a community of interests. We have sought to do this in a manner which, we believe, will help to bring from the Old World immigrants to our shores as the tide used to flow hither in the past, which will have the effect also of again bringing immigrants from the United States. We believe with the legislation we are presenting prosperity will return as it came in the days of the Liberal party before, when due regard was had to the development of the primary industries of this country. We feel we are helping to unite Canada, to promote a community of interest between the different classes and the different parts of our country, and in this way to build
up a stronger, a more prosperous and a happier Dominion, proud to be a part of the great British Empire to which we belong, a country that will be of service to its own kith and kin and of service as well to the community of nations of which it is a part..

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this late hour of the night and at this late stage of the debate I shall endeavour to make my contribution to the discussion as brief as possible I cannot let the occasion pass without saying a word of commendation to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the statement he submitted to the House five weeks ago to-day. My hon. friend is Scotch, and he has some of the valued characteristics of his race; he has the Scotch characteristic of hard-headedness, he has also the Scotch characteristic of modesty. But I think his modesty must really be suffering very severely in view of the lavish compliments that, quite properly, have been bestowed upon him. His budget speech was the shortest that has been delivered since I became a member of this House in 1917. That may be the reason why the debate is the longest in my parliamentary experience. If I might be permitted, I would proffer a word of advice to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to my right hon. friend who leads the opposition (Mr. Meighen); it is that in this respect they might each endeavour to emulate a little more the brevity followed by my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance in introducing his budget.
Nor can I let the occasion pass without saying a word with respect to the Minister of Finance (Mr Fielding) who is unable to be in his seat. I think by common consent the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding occupies a pre-eminent position in the public life of the Dominion. His experience as a public servant has extended' over forty years, commencing in the province of Nova Beotia and continuing in the larger federal arena. In that long and valuable service he has contributed unstintedly of his outstanding abilities to the upbuilding of this Dominion. I think it is a great deal to his credit that at the end. of that lengthy period of public service he stands at the forefront, remarkable for his courtesy to his opponents, and without the slightest suggestion of a stain on his reputation as a public man. In that respect he has set a worthy example to our public men, young and old, who may be moulding the destinies of the Dominion today, or in the future.
The Budget-Mr. Crerar

Turning to the 'budget itself, I wish to refer first to the national debt and) the surplus. I have not very closely analysed the statement produced by the Acting Minister of Finance as to whether it really shows a surplus or a deficit. I must confess that when I listened yesterday to my right hon. friend who leads the opposition I thought the surplus was vanishing into thin air, but when I listened again this afternoon to m3' right hon. friend who leads the government, I thought he presented another side of the story. But at any rate, what is the purpose of bookkeeping in a business concern or in our national economy? Its whole purpose is to reveal the precise and exact position of a business; and it should be so in regard to the affairs of the Dominion. I dare say that probably others could put a different construction after an analysis of the figures, to that which has already been given to the House. The important thing, however, is that the public should bo plainly and completely informed as to the exact position of our
10 p.m. finances. In respect to our railway financing I think its nature must govern its treatment in the national accounts. Anything in the nature of capital charges in the way of expenditure for railway extensions, for proper betterments, is a proper capital charge; there is a definite asset against it; and I see no good or sound reason why such should be charged up as a part of the ordinary expenditure of the country. That is the manner in which it has been treated in the past: all the guarantees that this country has given, to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars, has never been charged to the national debt. I could instance that in the guarantees that have been given to bodies like the Montreal Harbour Board, the Quebec Harbour Board, the Vancouver Harbour Board, and similar corporations; But there should be a- sharp distinction drawn between expenditure of that kind and expenditure that is incurred, for instance, in the form of capital charges on our railways.
It will be several years yet, probably two or three under the very best of conditions, before the earnings of the National Railways will be sufficient to pay operating expenses and all the charges against the money invested in the enterprise. The custom has been in the past to add these interest charges to the obligations of the road. These interest charges should be a direct charge on the finances of Canada until the road is in a position to meet them.
I want to make reference to a suggestion made by my hon. friend the member for

Brome (Mr. McMaster) in his admirable speech on the budget some days ago. In discussing the handling of the railway finances he advanced rather a novel idea. He made the suggestion that all the revenues of the railway should be paid into the consolidated fund of Canada, and that all the expenditures should be disbursed in the same way as other government expenditures are disbursed. Now I usually find myself in complete agreement with my hon. friend from Brome, but I am quite sure of this, that he has not given the suggestion that he made to the House very full study or consideration, or he would not have made it. That, to my mind, would make a wholly impossible condition of affairs in the administration of these roads. Fancy, for instance, having all the revenues that are taken in over all parts of this broad Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific paid into the consolidated revenue fund of Canada! How are the payments to be made? How are the expenses of the road to be met? The road could not possibly operate under those conditions with any satisfaction whatever. There would also be the further disadvantage that it would drive the administration of the road more and more into the ambit and orbit of political pressure and political consideration, and if this road is ever to succeed, and I believe it will succeed, it must be removed, absolutely and utterly, from the region of political interference.
I think there is some credit coming to the Acting Finance Minister (Mr. Robb) for the reductions in taxation that he has made. If press despatches are correct strong representations were made to the government prior to the delivery of the budget, that taxation should be reduced. But I have observed that the reductions that have been made through the budget we are now considering, affect altogether what might be termed the necessaries of life for the great masses 9f the Canadian people. I am among those who believe that taxation should be reduced in this country as rapidly as possible, and I am glad to see in the step the government have taken in that direction that they have reduced the taxes as far as possible on the things that are in most common use among the Canadian people, and that is certainly where taxes should be first reduced.
The chief issue involved in the budget, however, is the issue of the tariff. I listened with a great deal of interest to the address delivered by my right hon. friend who leads the opposition, and as well to my right hon, friend who leads the government. There is

The Budget-Mr. Crerar
no question whatever now where my hon. friends to my right stand on the question of the tariff.

speechtext: There never was.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, to be quite frank, when I was listening to the speech of my right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, yesterday afternoon, I had a doubt where he was going to come out on the question. But he evidently got some inspiration overnight and now he stands absolutely and flat-footedly on the principle of protection and not the tariff as we have it to-day. If there is any meaning in the words of my right hon. friend, they mean that if he is again returned to power and the party he leads resumes the reins of office in this country, there is no further chance of reductions in the tariff, but there is a certainty that the tariff will go up. My right hon. friend also had some criticism to offer of members of the Progressive party for having expressed different views on the tariff. Well, I presume that he will stand by the utterances of his own followers on this question. Only the other day, on May 12, the hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Hubbs), speaking from his seat in the House had this to say on the tariff:
'Now, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am entirely opposed to the budget. Let me emphasize again, what we must have in this country if we are going to build up Canada, is a good constructive tariff. If I had the framing of it I would say put on a tariff so high that nobody could fly over it with an aeroplane and so deep in its foundations that a submarine could not dig under it.
Now there is the real Simon-pure gospel of protection. I do not know how far my right hon. friend agrees with that, but I can tell him that th.e gospel that he preached this afternoon will not find a very favourable reception in that great part of Canada that lies west of the Great Lakes. But if the government's policy means anything, as enunciated by the Acting Minister of Finance, and as elaborated by the Prime Minister this afternoon, it means this, that the fiscal policy of this country, so far as the present government is concerned, is to be shaped in the future as it has been shaped in this budget, upon the principle of developing the great natural wealth of this Dominion. Now that, it seems to me, is a distinct step in advance, and I will endeavour to show why a little bit later.
Some reference has been made in the debate to the Liberal platform of 1919. Well, I remember reading the press descriptions of that great convention, at which were assembled delegates from every constituency in Canada. They gathered here in Ottawa
from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and it was not the leaders of the Liberal party at that time who were making the platform of the party. That was a democratic convention, so far as my recollection goes, and so far as my reading of newspaper reports of its proceedings is concerned, and that convention, embracing some seven or eight hundred delegates from all over this Dominion, sat down in consideration of a course of public policy. Whether the government that was elected in 1921, and which my right hon. friend now leads, has up to the present lived up to that platform or not, I think they may justly claim that in the present tariff proposals which they have brought down they have at any rate made a step in that direction.
Why do I offer a word of commendation of this budget? Because this budget recognizes the position of agriculture in this great Dominion. I have advocated in this House on several occasions before-I advocated it during the election of 1921 in every constituency, I think, in which I spoke-that a sound fiscal policy for Canada was a policy which would develop the natural wealth of the country, which would not endeavour to foster and stimulate, at the expense of the great masses of the people, artificial industries that were unsuitable to the development of this Dominion. Sir, I believe that that policy is sound to-day, and sounder to-day than it has ever been before. Our protectionist friends argue that we should be a great manufacturing country, that we should manufacture our own raw materials in Canada and export the finished product abroad. I have no fault to find with that. But what value is a protective tariff in the development of manufacturing industries based on the natural resources of this country when we produce from these resources away and above what we can possibly consume at home? I ask what value is a protective tariff to an industry of that kind? What value is a protective tariff, to the great pulp and lumber industry of this country? Take the figures of our exports and they are growing almost every year in that particular industry. What value is a protective tariff, for instance, to the flour milling industry of this country? We export hundreds of thousands of barrels of flour every year from Canada. What benefit is it to a meat packing establishment? What benefit is it to any of the great industries that are based on our natural resources? It is of no benefit. But where has the protective tariff been invoked in Canada, where has it been used? It has been used in building up or creating industries in Canada the major portion of which depend
The Budget-Mr. Crerar

upon a foreign country for their raw material. I submit, Sir, that that is not a sound method of development.
After all, where does the great wealth, the real wealth, of this country lie? It lies in our fertile fields, it lies in our vast mineral areas, in our forest wealth, and in our fisheries: and if we are to seek and find a sane and sound policy of national development we must seek it along the lines that will encourage production of wealth from these things, and not by the creation and stimulation of artificial industries that depend upon foreign countries for their raw material. I might instance some of these. Take the most highly protected things in this country and what are they? Well, we find them in cotton goods, we find them in rubber goods, and we find them also in many other lines. Is it a sane policy-I ask my protectionist friends this question-to penalize the people of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to increase the cost of living to every person in this Dominion, to build up industries of this character? I say it is not a sane policy. That is why I am in support of the policy the government has brought down as far as it has gone.
Now, this budget has not really hurt any one. Who has it hurt?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has hurt a lot of feeling.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has hurt a lot of feeling. The reductions in duties on agricultural implements have been compensated for, and rightly so, by the reductions on the raw materials that go into those implements. And what is the net result? The net result to-day is that every farmer in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, will buy his agricultural implements this year cheaper than before, or cheaper than he otherwise would have done if this budget had not been brought down. I am at a loss to understand the attitude of many newspapers and public men, and I might include in that the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition because of the course he has taken on this question. I read something not very long ago about "the influence of the psychology of fear." That is the attitude of mind to-day of some people. If you study this thing in the light of the cold analysis of fact what injury has it done? And yet we have a tremendous outcry all over the greater part of Ontario and part of Quebec. I am amused in reading the Montreal Star. A few months ago it had a series of editorials under the caption "The whisper of death." It saw nothing but

blue ruin, and now it sees nothing but blue ruin from this budget'. I can compliment my right hon. friend who leads the opposition on one thing-that his speech here today has probably brought him the support of the Montreal Star, and that, I am sure, will be a great joy to his heart. I shall watch very anxiously and with a great deal of care for its editorials to-morrow.
But this brings back to my mind the reciprocity arrangement of 1911. What injury was done to the Canadian manufacturers under that arrangement? There was not a single possible injury to them under the reciprocity arrangement of 1911; it would in the end have been a boon to them. But what was the course taken? Well, we had the manifesto of the "noble eighteen" of Toronto who came out in flat-footed opposition. We had a frenzy and furor of opposition to that proposal created for months by active propaganda in eastern Cnada. And with what result? That the people of Canada were misled as to the real purpose and real value of that arrangement. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has argued that that arrangement would have been of no value to Canada, that we were far better without it, and some of his supporters have taken the same ground. Was it of no value to this country with its tremendous agricultural output to find! all the possible markets that could be found for these agricultural products? On the very face of it was that not a common sense proposal? In a study of our national economy what this country needs more than anything else at the present time is markets, and under the reciprocity arrangement of 1911 we were given access to the American market for our natural products.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What was the response from your own province of Manitoba in regard to that?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh yes, I have heard that question before and I answered it. I want to say to my hon. friend now that he got a response from the province of Manitoba in 1921 as to what it thinks on the question of reciprocity and the question of tariff generally. In Canada we were robbed of the benefits of that arrangement. My right hon. friend argues that there would have been no stability to that arrangement, that we could not depend on the United States government living up to its obligations; but the fact was that the American government kept that offer on its statute books for over ten years

The Budget-Mr. Crerar
It incorporated it into the law of the United States, and it remained there until they became convinced of the fact that Canada had slammed the door in their faces and did not want to have anything to do with them. The agitation that has been worked up over the budget in eastern Canada reminds me of the agitation worked up against reciprocity in 1911.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It did not frighten you?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it did not frighten me. Let me say a further word or two about the reciprocity pact in 1911. That arrangement gave entry to the United States market for our wheat and live stock. Every additional dollar that could be brought into Canada as a result of the sale of these products was an additional dollar of purchasing power on the farms of Canada for the business concerns of this Dominion. I am amused at the attitude I find in eastern Canada on this budget. I was interested recently in reading an article in the Hamilton Herald, an interview with the president-I take it the president of the local branch of the manufacturers' association in the city of Hamilton-given out after the budget was delivered by the Acting Finance Minister (Mr. Robb). The article says:
It is very far reaching and is giving the western farmer, who is really a foreigner an award at the expense of the other parts of the Dominion.. The western farmer as a rule has no interest in the country. He eats out of a can and gets all he can from outside the country, and puts his wheat in in the spring. As soon as he harvests and markets his grain he goes off to California, or some other place for the winter, and spends his money outside the country.
Here is a new definition of a western farmer. He is a foreigner who eats out of a can and winters in California. That is an interview given to the Hamilton Herald by the president of the local manufacturers' association. I have here another paper, the Labour Leader, of Toronto and I would commend this to my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). I shall not read the article in full; in fact, I shall do no more than draw attention to it. But the whole purpose of the article is to excite indignation, to stir up people, and to work them up to a high pitch of opposition to any reductions in the tariff that may give any benefit to agriculture.
I desire to say a word or two as to the attitude of the West on this question of tariff, and why western Canada holds the view it does hold on the tariff. What are the chief products of western Canada? The chief products of that part of the Dominion are agricultural products. We produce grain in large quantities. We produce live stock, butter,
wool and the other agricultural products that are commonly found in agricultural communities. The wheat production of western Canada last year reached 480,000,000 bushels. We will require to export at least 380,000,000 bushels of that crop either in wheat or in flour. We sell that wheat to the markets of the world, in competition with the countries of the world. We also produce live stock in great number and our production of live animals is away In excess of the possible consumption of this Dominion. What is the basis upon which the prices for these commodities are fixed? They are fixed also in the markets of the world in competition with the world, and the same is true with regard to our dairy products, and all our agricultural products. What value then is your protective tariff to the western Canadian farmer.
I mention this fact, sir, because I think there is a great deal of misunderstanding in eastern Canada as to the actual position of the West on this question of tariff. The western farmer is not a protectionist and never will be; I will say more, that you can take the most hidebound protectionist you can find in Ontario, in Montreal or anywhere else; and send him to western Canada, and while the heresy may cling to him as long as he lives because of his early environment and training, yet none of his children will grow up to believe in it. After all people's views on questions of this kind are fixed or influenced largely by their local conditions, and environment, and you cannot convince the western farmer, nor can you convince the average western businessman in town or city, that a protective tariff is of any value to him. I was glad to hear a reference by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the concluding portion of his remarks as to the need of unity in this Dominion.
After all the most significant political fact in Canada to-day is the thousand miles of wilderness between the East and the West. As legislators in this parliament we should never lose sight of the fact that what we really have in this Dominion is two or three separate communities, and one of the greatest tasks of statesmanship in the Dominion is to shape policies, and find policies that will hold this country together. It is not enough to say to the western people, "You are ungrateful; we have assisted in creating the country for you and you are ungrateful when you protest against a protective tariff." That will not convince them, but I do believe that the western people in general outlook are reasonable, notwithstanding the criticism that has been directed against them. It is true the great mass of the western people
The Budget-Mr. Crerar

have pretty definite views on this question of the tariff. I realize in any solution of it, there may require to be something of the principle of give and take. The idea that exists among many eastern manufacturers and industries that western Canada is out to destroy industry is wholly wrong. It is not the case, but we must realize the fact that western Canada does not profit in any way from a protective tariff. I say in all seriousness that that fact should be realized and understood in eastern Canada, if a way is to be found that will prevent any serious conflict of opinion arising on this question as between different parts of the Dominion. I speak quite frankly, speaking only for myself, when I say that if the tariff is fixed on a basis of the revenue needs of the country, it should be possible to'find such a way. The revenue requirements of this country mean that revenue must be raised through the agency of the tariff for many years to come. There is no gainsaying that fact; but I want to repeat that a tariff based on the principle and the needs of revenue is a wholly different thing from a tariff based on the principle of protection.
We have had a good many arguments in this debate from hon. members who believe in the principle of protection, that it is essential to the building up of this country, that a protective tariff is the great contributor to the wealth of this country. After all, what is the best measure or gauge of the wealth t>f a country? It is the volume and character of its trade, with other countries, not the volume it does in trading amongst its own individuals. What are the facts in respect to the trade of the Dominion when it enters the world's market? Let us take the figures for the twelve months ended March 31, last, as prepared by the Department of Customs and Excise. We find this:
Exports of Dominion
Agricultural and vegetable	products.. .. $391,000,000
Animals and animal products	 140,000,000
Agricultural and vegetable products, other
than foods	 39,000,000
Wood, wood products and	paper	 273.000,000
And so on. I quote these figures merely to show that the real source of wealth in this Dominion comes from its agricultural lands, its forests and its fisheries.	.
I do not wish to delay the House, and I want to pass on and to consider briefly the argument that has been urged by our protectionist friends that we should have a self-contained country; in other words, that we should endeavour to live as much as possible within ourselves. There is no such thing anywhere in the world to-day as a selLcontained country. Reference has been made in the discussion before, I believe by the hon. mem-
ber for South Winnipeg (Mr Hudson), to the position of Great Britain. Where is there in the world to-day a country that excels Great Britain in prosperity, a country that has stood the shock of war and the reconstruction period following the war as well as Great Britain? But is she a self-contained country? Great Britain has not at any time food supplies to last her for more than six or eight weeks. She imports raw cottons, raw materials in a multitude of ways, and it is by manufacturing and re-exporting them and trading with the world that she has amassed her great wealth. And with what result? Only recently the Chancellor of the Exchequer brought down his budget and he showed a reduction in their debt for the year of over $240,000,000. What is the position of protectionist Germany, of protectionist France to-day?-one asking the world to help rehabilitate her; the other in a perilous position financially.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member think that western farmers who are complaining to-day would better their condition by emigrating to Great Britain?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not really know what that has to do with the case. I do not think they would. I do not see why they should do so. The fact is that there are too many people in Great Britain to-day. The British government are subsidizing them to get them away.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the same thing happen here if we had free trade in Canada?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks if the same thing would happen here if we had free trade in Canada. With a country 5,000 miles in extent from ocean to ocean and anywhere from nothing to 1,000 miles north of inhabitable territory we could support a hundred million people without any difficulty.
The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) had something to say about the Americanization of Canadian industry. He argues that, as a result of these tariff changes the manufacturing business of this Dominion will go to the United States; that our industries would be all Americanized, and that our people would be leaving Canada in shoals as a result of the proposals brought down by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). What are the facts in respect to the movement of population to the United States? It is true that within the last few years we have had a considerable movement of population from Canada to the United States, but that movement took place before this budget was brought down. If we go back

The Budget-Mr. Crerar
a little bit into the history of Canada, I find on examination that, in the period 1880 to 1890, which is the period immediately following the inauguration of the National Policy of protection which was put into effect in Canada in 1878 or 1879, ^t a time when the population of this Dominion was about one-half of what it is at the present time, more than 392,000 people left Canada to go to the United States. If we examine the figures further, we find that from the late nineties for the next ten or twelve years there was practically no movement of population from Canada to the United States. What was the reason of that? It was this, that western Canada was opening up; great quantities of free land were available to settlers who were coming in and taking advantage of that. The movement was from . eastern Canada to our western provinces. As regards the Americanization of our industries, I should like to draw attention to this fact, that that process is going on at the present time in any case. What are the facts? Today American capital is flowing into this country in immense quantities, and that is perfectly agreeable to my hon. friends to my right. The industries of the Dominion are to-day largely controlled by American capital. A statement issued by the Bankers' Trust Company of New York, a short time ago, gave the information that over $2,500,000,000 of American money was invested in the Dominion of Canada. In 1921, more than SI,- 000,000,000 was invested in fifteen groups engaged in manufacturing enterprises in Canada. What does this mean? My hon. friends to my right do not want Canadians to buy American made goods; they want the American to come over here with his capital, to establish himself in Canada and to make the goods in this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

My hon. friend says:
"hear, hear," but the result of that is this, that he comes over here and he becomes the most ardent advocate there is for a protective tariff in this Dominion.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend again says:
" hear, hear " to that fact. As a result of that, the American capitalist comes to Canada under the aegis of our protective tariff. He gets his return on his investment; he takes that back to his own country, and the people of Canada from one end of the country to the other have contributed to that result.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He pays a large amount of wages.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He pays a certain amount in wages, and the raw materials are found in this country. Now, there is one other result so far as the principle of protection in the tariff is concerned, and that is that it leads inevitably to the development of state socialism; it is a form of state socialism. When the power of the state is used to give benefits to a certain section of the people through tariff laws it is a direct use of that power to benefit a portion of the community at the expense of the rest. Reference has been made in this debate to the condition of agriculture in western Canada and throughout the Dominion, and the argument is advanced that what agriculture needs in this country is more protection. The United States is a highly protected country; and what is the position of agriculture there? With all their protection agriculture is in a worse condition in the United States than it is in Canada. And what is the inescapable result? The American farmer is appealing to congress for relief and proposals are before that body for the expenditure of vast sums of money to afford relief to the farmers of the United States who find that they cannot prosper under their present system.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend admit that in England under free trade since 1846 the British farmers have been nearly wiped out of existence?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If they have been nearly
wiped out of existence, it is because of another reason altogether. If my hon. friend would talk with British farmers as I have to many of those who have come to western Canada he would find out why they leave the Old Country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They left to come to a protected country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense; they left because they could not pay the exorbitant rents which the landlords asked them to pay.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Conservative landlords.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are a few other
points which I think should be touched upon. I believe that this country needs strong constructive policies at the present time, and I purpose supporting the budget because I think it is a step in the right direction. At the same time, if my right hon. friend who leads the government gets his tariff advisory
The Budget-Mr. Crerar

committee at. work one of the first duties which I think that committee should undertake will be to find out for instance why it is that the duty is fixed at 20 per cent, on shovels and spades and 30 per cent on bathtubs and dishpans. There should be a consistent principle running through the establishment of a tariff policy in Canada, and it is for the people through their government to settle what that principle shall be. With the principle upon which your tariff is to be based once established, then I think there may be some advantage in having a body such aS the Prime Minister referred to; but that body should be charged with further duties than those of advising on the ironing out inequalities in the tariff. One of the most necessary things in the Dominion to-day is some study of the whole question of taxation in order to prevent overlapping in the imposition of taxes, and a study of the incidence of provincial and federal taxation. After all, we cannot get away from the fact that the country is facing grave difficulties. While our debt is enormous I believe we have the resources that will overcome our handicaps from the taxation that we have to support. But this can be done only by the most intelligent study of the whole problem, and I think that some such body charged with the duty of studying the whole question of taxation could give a great deal of information to the government and to the country that would assist in getting taxation established on a fair, sound basis.
I am satisfied with the budget as far as it goes; but, if I may repeat what I said a little while ago, I believe that a basis can be found upon which we can get some common agreement between East and West on the question of the tariff by placing the tariff frankly on a revenue basis and recognizing it as such and not as a protective tariff. There must yet be very considerable reductions in the tariff. No one wants to hurt Canadian industry, and least of all do the people of western Canada desire to do so. But I say that the task of statesmanship in Canada is to find policies that will hold the country together, that will unite it from one end to the other. We can have our differences of opinion on administration, and we doubtless shall have such differences in the future. But I deprecate, I deplore anything that will arise in this Canada of ours that will fix our political differences on sectional or racial considerations. Let us avoid that altogether. It is because I think that the government, in the step that it has taken in

the budget in reducing the taxation on implements of production, is pursuing a sound policy and one which I believe will conduce to harmony in the Dominion, that I intend to support the budget when the vote is taken.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While there have been many references in the course of this long debate to the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is not present with us on this occasion, I do not think it would be at all out of place for me, coming in a sense from the section of the country from which he comes, to express again the feeling of regret which this House and the country experiences that a man who has been so long prominent in Canadian public life, a man with whom we do not all pretend to agree-for we cannot expect such unanimity in political matters-yet a man who has won our respect for his courage, his directness and the great ability he has displayed during many years, is not able, through unfortunate illness, to participate in what to him was probably the greatest happiness of his life, namely, parliamentary work. We must always expect in the course of life that incidents of this character will occur; and I can never avoid thinking, when it does occur in the course of a strenuous political life, of the words of the great poet who depicted what comes into the life of almost every man when he says:
...in the open noon of my pride
They sent me a voice from the darkness;
They whispered and called me aside.
They said, "the end is forbidden;" They said, "thy use is fulfilled."
And to those of us who may be permitted to remain perhaps for years in the active work of the nation will some day come the summons to that enforced rest which always seems to come unexpectedly, and which evokes in such an assembly as the Parliament of Canada that warm and deep and honest sympathy which has been expressed from either side of the House towards the absent member.
In a purely personal sense I join in the tribute that has been paid to his acting successor (Mr. Robb). I can at least congratulate the acting minister on the brevity of the remarks with which he introduced the budget. I agree with the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) that it would have been well if that brevity had been emulated by many succeeding speakers, but I fear before I get through to-night that I too may be counted among those who have somewhat failed to copy that extreme brevity which characterized the introduction of the budget. I will, however, do my best to economize time.

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
In passing, may I remark on the absence from the House this evening of a gentleman who used to be considered in political circles as a probable successor to the Minister of Finance should a vacancy occur in that post. We have not with us to-night the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell), nor have we any explanation of his absence. No doubt there is a reason, a potent and a valid reason; and while I enjoyed the mock heroics of my right hon. friend the leader of the government when he declared there would be no general election, ' and that the people of Canada were so contented and happy under his beneficent rule that there would be no need for a general election, I could not help but think that at all events he will have the benefit of a record of public opinion in an important part of the Dominion as the logical and necessary political consequence of the withdrawal from this chamber of the hon. member for St. Antoine.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are so many other
questions besides the budget upon which public attention could be challenged that I almost wonder at the temerity of an hon. gentleman on the other side suggesting the possibility of additional reasons for the government asking the country for that public confidence which no longer remains with it. I sympathize with the temporary successor of the Minister of Finance. He is walking with stumbling feet along a path which he does not know, driven by the impulsion of a blind opportunism which has already destroyed a great historic party that once had a record of achievement behind it and a set of principles by which it believed the Canadian commonwealth could be best regulated. But to-day the right hon. Prime Minister is no longer leading a great historic party. His traditional Liberalism has faded into invisible distance and the real direction of the affairs of Canada is coming from the group which is seated to my left; the wreck and the rump of the Liberal party follows along the path that is blazed by the hon. member for Marquette and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). It is a great price-some of us would think too great-to pay for the temporary enjoyment of office, but hon. gentlemen opposite us do not apparently so regard it. They probably think it is cheap. The public sooner or later will have an opportunity of pronouncing judgment, and we will then realize where they think the real cheapness is.
I	do not propose to follow at any painful length the speakers who have preceded me in a discussion of the supposititious surplus which has been presented to the House. I have heard some discussion of bookkeeping methods, and I think if I caught them aright I am tolerably in agreement with the remarks of the hon. member for Marquette, who thinks it would be better to place on public record in a definite way the obligations of the country. I have listened, not without amazement and not without some impatience, to the most extraordinary references that were made by the right hon. Prime Minister and some others to the reasons for treating the advances to the Canadian National Railways as something other than a part of the public debt. I wonder if hon. gentlemen opposite have ever stopped for a moment to think quietly of what constitutes the real difference between the cases cited by the right hon. gentleman and the present case. We are told that when a dry dock has been
subsidized or a loan made to a
II	p.m. railway company, as very frequently has been done in the history of Canada, that that is an interestbearing advance, and does not properly become a portion of the public debt. That seems to be quite true. But is there any possible reasonable analogy between a case such as that and the financial transactions of the past years? I fail to see it. Let us try to get the thing down to the basis of a purely homely illustration. Suppose that a man has a house and some land on which he has from time to time expended $100,000; suppose that the actual present value of the property is not one penny more than $10,000; and suppose that he has outstanding obligations for his $100,000; then let him go into the market and ask someone to lend him $1,000 on a mortgage of that property. Can he get it? Yes, but not on the property; he can get it on the personal security of individuals who are worth a sufficient margin above the amount he wishes to borrow. Now to my mind that is exactly where we are with reference to the Canadian National Railway system. We have a congeries of railways brought together into one vast system with a debt immensely exceeding the present or possible future value of the property, and no money loaned to that system can get any adequate security. Who in the world of finance would to-night lend one dollar on that railway without some collateral security? But what do they do? Something that has been very common to all of us in political life.

The Budget-Mr. Baxter

Somebody comes and says:	I have not got
any credit at the bank, but the manager says if you will put your name on the back of a piece of paper he will be most happy to make the advance. By analogy, the lender of the money comes to the Dominion government and says:	If the people of Canada
will put their collective name on the back of a piece of paper the money will be forthcoming. Now, that is what you do when you guarantee any loan on account of the Canadian National Railway system. There is no security in the railway; the security is in the tax-paying power of the people of Canada, and nowhere else, and the only honest thing, the only proper thing, from a bookkeeping standpoint or any other standpoint, is to honestly and properly charge that up as an additional debt upon the people of Canada. I shall not spend any further time upon that. We were told by the right hon. the Prime Minister to-day that that was a matter of no importance, and he launched into, shall I say, a very satisfactory statement to himself of that increase in trade that had taken place in the last few years. Was that due, * in any way, to this government, Mr. Speaker? Did he expect after the war period was over that the world and Canada was going to stand absolutely still? We had had far greater trade expansion during the war years, and we know the reasons for that expansion. Then came the falling-off. Did he expect that there never would' be any recovery? Some recovery has fortunately accrued to Canada, but how much greater would that recovery have been had the business interests of Canada been assured of some reasonable stability in the financial policy of this country?
He passed on and discussed the reduction in taxes. I shall spend but little time on that. He told us, as others have told us, that that reduction will be $24,000,000. The only estimate we have been able to get has come from the Finance department, and it is that the reduction in duties will only amount to $750,000. Will any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, or will any hon. gentleman sitting to my left, sitting there in control of the side of the House which is on the right, tell us that $23,250,000 will be economized by the reductions in the sales tax? I do not think I will find anyone with the hardihood to make such an assertion as that. If there is to be a reduction of $24,000,000, why has not some gentleman in the course of this tremendously long debate come forward and given us some kind of tabulated definite estimate of the particular things which will achieve this reduction? Oh,

but it suits them far better to go out to the public and talk of $24,000,000. I will venture to predict, and I am not at all fond of the role of prophecy, that when they come back ^ here next year we shall not hear of a reduction in taxation of $24,000,000 or if we do, we will have a worse financial statement than any that has preceded it.
The right hon. gentleman also undertook to illuminate the want of financial capacity of the previous government. He dilated on the assertion that has repeatedly been made from the other side of the House, that Canada did not bear any portion of the war cost during the period of the war. That is the way, I am putting it precisely, the assertion was made and repeated over and over again in the course of this debate, and in the course of another debate which took place in this House. But .the right hon. the leader of the government discovers now that we paid only some of the interest on the war debt, and he charges now that the old government did not pay part of the capital cost while the war was in progress. If it were not for the frenzy of politics, would hon. members see any real distinction? Let me come to that again by way of a very simple illustration. When a public work is undertaken, everyone knows, the interest during construction is charged as a part of construction, and is properly so charged. Unfortunately, what the whole world was doing during four years was paying the cost of destruction instead of construction, and they had to pay, most regrettably, interest upon the cost of destruction. Can you distinguish that from the capital cost? Is there any difference? And yet it is manifest in the figures that the old government bore some part of the cost of destruction that was being incurred during those perilous years. There is no use mincing words about it, no use inventing new phrases, no use trying to draw some inferences to the discredit of gentlemen on this side of the House. The fact remains that the cost of the war that was passed on after the old government went out of office was less than the total cost of the war to Canada, and therefore some part of it had been paid during the period in which my right hon. leader or his predecessor was the leader of the government.
Then we were told further, that the reduction of the cost of living was the great aim of the Liberal party. If that be so, unless the Liberal party had its genesis with the advent to power of the right hon. the Prime Minister, when that Liberal party was led by' Sir Wilfrid Laurier and assisted by the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, I would like to ask why

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
they did [DOT] not abolish the tariff in those pre-war days when the whole tariff could have been abolished with far less strain from a financial standpoint upon the people than is involved in a very small disturbance of taxation at the present time. When we are dealing now with hundreds of millions of dollars to run this country we can see how, when it took less than $100,000,000 to run the country, they could, if that had been the real aim of the Liberal party, have got along with some internal revenue taxes, some income tax and sales taxes and done without protection, which they are proposing to destroy root and branch with a pair of tweezers, nipping off a little each year.
But it is like everything else that comes from the government, it is entirely unsatisfactory. It is only meant for a bit of camouflage; it is only meant to delude some people and to obtain a temporary anchorage in some political haven that perhaps appears, and appears only on that magical chart by which the leader of the government is professing to steer the country, and which no one else has ever seen. If Mr. Speaker, you follow the advice of my good friend and take the burdens off production, he tells you that the producer can produce more and at lower costs. Well, there are a good many producers, but will my right hon. friend explain to the country where are the markets for the producers? He has heard very largely from the group sitting to my left that they are producing more today than they can get sale for, and they keep on producing. But there are other things in Canada than the production of wheat, and if we are to take the burdens off production so that the producer can produce more, I want to find out a little something about the consumer. That is a matter of some importance to the country. I want to know, and this country has got to know, and has got to make up its mind whether it wants the consumer to dwell within the limits of Canada, or whether it proposes that the consumer shall dwell only in some part of the United States.
That after all marks the absolute line of cleavage between this party and the party and a half with whom we are in conflict in this House and in this country. Shall we have a home market that is worth having? Shall we bring people into this country, provide the means for their employment, build up industries within Canada, make it a country worth living in, and in that way develop the agricultural interests of the Dominion? Or shall we, gradually or by one bound, obliterate all traces of industry and thereby make what 137i
was the home market of Canada consist in exporting goods from this country to reach citizens who have been exported a little in advance of the goods. But the right hon. Prime Minister does not tell me where the markets are. Instead of that what do I get? A rhythmical treatise delivered in splendid language on the four essentials of land, labour, capital, and management. He hesitated a little over the management. First of all he said there were three essentials, and then he stated there were four. He was sure of the land, the labour and the capital, but after a short period of doubt he decided to include the management. I know why the doubt was. It was not a philosophic doubt, it was a real, actual one that time. Having had an experience of his own government since December, 1921, he doubted if there was such a thing as management of this country. About that disquisition there was a faint aroma of the class room. One could almost imagine the campus of a college largely endowed by the Rockefeller millions. You could see the students assembled there and you could almost hear their cheering, led by some professor, when the happy news would come to the college that John D. had opened another oil gusher on some part of this world's surface. It was an unreal thing; it was the sort of thing that you get at an institution of learning; it was not a real practical sort of thing that has to be dealt with in this House and in the government of the country -wholly academic, while God knows what the world to-day needs is the thing that is practical. When we have shown the world how to do its work and how to solve its problems, some twenity-five years afterwards the universities will begin to write books about it and tell the people how it was done. The solution of the problems of the world comes from the working men of the world first and finds its way into the universities afterwards.
Then my right hon. friend passed to the basic implements of production, but he did not follow them very far. He dodged the lawn mowers, they were not apparently basic. He tarried a while with the farmers. It- was basic there because it was political. It was the basic thing that gives a basic majority in a House where they would not have a scintilla of power unless they reached out and treated your opponents better than they have-treated their friends. That is the position of the right hon. Prime Minister: He has sacrificed, he is sacrificing-and fifteen of his supporters from Nova Scotia are daily and nightly parties to the sacrifice-the best interests of the Maritime provinces in the matter of the steel and the coal industry be-
The Budget-Mr. Baxter

cause the Prime Minister has seen fit to pay no attention to the claims, the legitimate claims, of the part of the country that gave him its support when he turned to the three western provinces that had rejected him and paid them with some reduction in the duty on farming implements. He had a solid sixteen to join in this iniquity. Since the people of Halifax had the opportunity of speaking it is only a solid fifteen; and the sooner the constituencies are opened in Nova Scotia the sooner the Prime Minister will find what the people, not the politicians, of that part of the country think of his performance.

I found him the other
night interfering with the political organism of the Secretary of State. They did not seem to be entirely in harmony, and I notice that the Secretary of State has been looking rather anaemic since the attack of my hon. friend. I rather agreed with my hon. friend too. Microbes are useful under certain circumstances.
Well, as a result of this wonderful budget a few tools are made free for the miner but the market is left to be invaded by the alien. I suppose a few shovels, and possibly a few shovel handles are affected. I do not know whether they have yet got as far as the handles that the coal miner may use in a pit in Cape Breton but his product is not protected, not adequately protected against the ravages of [DOT] American competition. And the railway rates remain so that he cannot send his product into the central portion of Canada under favourable conditions. My hon. friends opposite have done far more for the wheat miner than they have done for

the coal miner, and in doing it for the wheat miner they did it with the boisterous applause of fifteen members from a solid Nova Scotia.
