speechtext:
He is going again. I am a little bit interested, and I know that my hon. friend who interrupted me is interested, and that there are fourteen others on his side of the House, whether they are physically present or not, who are very much interested in the development of the native and natural industries of Nova Scotia. Though I come from New Brunswick I feel that I am quite as much interested because the hour has come when the Maritime provinces must stand together in order to get a fair show from the rest of the people of Canada in reference to their development. I am going to quote-and I can quote with approval- a portion of a speech made by the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) speaking at Stellarton, Friday, October 26, 1921. He said:
Last year one hundred million of good Canadian money was paid to the United States for coal under this protective tariff-this peculiar tariff which they say you must not lay any unholy hands upon.
My hon. friend was then running in opposition to the Meighen government. I am not going to entirely endorse the abuse that he uttered in this speech, but I am going to agree with the sense and purport of it. He continues:
One hundred million dollars we paid out, while at the same time people here could not sell their coal and our mines were working two or three days a week. Do you want these conditions to continue? If you do you will vote for my opponent, and he has no solution for the situation other than that.
I commend that to all good Nova Scotians of the Liberal party. They must have agreed it was good doctrine. They ought to agree it is good doctrine still. My hon. friend was discussing Colonel Cantley, his opponent, and he said1:
Do you want to send a man to Ottawa that, when he gets there, will turn around and say: " I gave you no pledges, I never said to you I would take this course or that on any question. All I said was, " There is a tariff in this country and I do not want to see it removed."
Hon. gentlemen will remark how much difference it makes whether a nebulous statement is uttered by Colonel Cantley or by the present Prime Minister. In the one case it is condemned and in the other it is worshipped, and it is even repeated to the drum roll of applause, hour after hour, in this House, as has been done on this very occasion. My hon. friend the Minister of National Defence did not think it was right when it came to Colonel Cantley. He said:
That is not a proper course for any man under responsible government who asks the suffrages of a people. I have had long experience in public life and I say that a man who seeks the suffrages of the people should be prepared to come before them, state his policy, pledge himself as to what he is prepared to do, and when grave situations arise be in a position to have some justification for actions to be taken in order that these conditions may be changed.	.
Then my hon. friend 'challenged the audience and said:
What do you think of maintaining a duty on wheat and flour? Why should there be a tariff to enable the men who grind the flour to grind the * faces of the poor. I am opposed to the duty on flour.
The hon. gentleman is a member of the government now. I look, I watch, and I wait, for some sign of carrying into effect this solemn declaration which he made to the people of his own constituency. It was the advice of a true Progressive who spoke, but I find1 he has not yet joined the majority of the government. He continues:
I pledge myself if I go back to Ottawa-
And he did.
-to represent this county to advocate in parliament and insist upon the fact that the people of Ontario, if they want to burn coal which is not produced in Canada, that they should contribute to the revenue of the country by paying a tariff on it. And so, my friends, I am not like Colonel Cantley-unwilling to give pledges. I tell you if I go to Ottawa I shall urge parliament to put a duty on coal that is a real duty and not a fake duty.
My hon. friend came to parliament. He is in parliament now. He has been advanced in parliament. He is in this House to-night, and I give him the opportunity of telling us if there has been any change in the coal duties except to allow the dust from lignite coal to come in free and lignite coke. These are the only changes. He was a wonderful power in Nova Scotia, a tower of strength to the Liberal party, but how futile when he reaches the atmosphere of this House. He cannot do a thing for his constituency. Why it would have been better to have elected Colonel Cantley without his pledges than to have elected the Minister of National Defence with all his promises. But I want to go back for a minute or two to my right hon. friend
The Budget-Mr. Baxter

the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). He referred to a wide spreading tree this afternoon, with beautiful branches, and he saw those branches all rising at the stump. Well in a wooden country we do not see the branches coming from the stump. When you find the stump the tree is gone. He may have seen the bole of the tree or the trunk, but the stump, comes there after the tree has been destroyed. Well, this is the tree that he saw. He has been seeing these visions and dreaming these dreams. He saw this tree denuded of its sap. Somebody took the sap away near the base of the tree, near that stump. He apparently was not familiar enough with forest life in Canada-forest life perhaps was not philosophical enough-to know that you can drain sap from the tree which is the national emblem of the country, and it can be made profitable to the community without injuring the tree. In the same sense we can, I believe, have protection in Canada without destroying the tree of my - right hon. friend's vision. But he descanted so much upon the tree that it made me really wonder whether he had not gone back to extremely early times and imagined himself to be the first if not the only man in the world. He may have thought of that tree of knowledge of good and evil of which we read. He apparently had gone so far as to taste the fruits of it. He had become conscious in a traditional sense, and in order to cover his political nakedness he spent about an hour in piecing together newspaper clippings in order to make a sort of garb with which to cover himself, and that as a contribution to the budget debate of the country. I would remind him that people who meddle with the tree of knowledge of good and evil are pursued by a flaming sword and driven from the paradise in which they have temporarily taken refuge. Give the people of Canada one fair chance, and the angel with the flaming sword will forever bar his return to those precincts in the Eastern block where weary legislators refresh themselves in the afternoon with a cup of invigorating tea. But with more fire still he inveighed against protection for what he called a few special interests. I want to ask, not this House-it is not worth while really asking this House- but this country, whether my right hon. friend has scotched the snake of the special interests to which he has referred so much, or has completely killed it? We spent some time in developing special legislation at his instance directed against trusts and combines; the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) was brandishing a battle-axe; something was going to crash in this country; the people were absolutely 
afraid because of the investigating powers that were given; but we were assured that all that was necessary was to get plenty of light and publicity, and these noxious weeds would disappear from Canadian public life. I have not yet heard of a trust or combine that has been rooted out by this government. I have heard of some towards the fostering of which I thought they contributed. I remember, during the last election campaign, the way in which former Attorney General Raney of Ontario inveighed against trusts, combines and everything else connected with automobiles, but I have not seen the automobile snake even scotched yet by the vigour of this government. I have not found any other trusts or combines attacked. What was all this legislation for? Did they know of these things before they came into power? If they did, why did they not get after them? If they did not know of them and only suspected them, why are we not made cognizant of the efforts that they have made since coming into power to drive these things out of our economic life? The sum total of the matter is that it is like almost everything else that distinguished the campaign of my hon. friends and that distinguishes their political course at the present day; it is nothing but camouflage, nothing but deception, a hollow mockery, a beating of the sounding drum, in an effort to arouse public attention hoping that it will be in its favour.
Then, credit is claimed and volubly claimed for a reduction in the sales tax. Time forbids that I should go into any painful discussion of the sales tax to-night; but I would ask, as one of the minor questions-and it is an important one in some of our Maritime constituencies-why it is that canned vegetables are exempted from the sales tax, but canned fish are subject to 5 per cent, which is now the maximum sales tax? Does this government solemnly recommend people to eat vegetables and eschew fish? I wonder how the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) views that proposition.
I always thought a mixed diet was good, together with a little something you cannot get in Toronto.

That is just what I want
to get, the chance to mix the diet, but the poor consumer has to bear, on an absolute foodstuff, a 5 per cent tax if it is canned sardines or fish of any kind. Vegetables, he can get free, but on sardines he has to pay the tax. Yet this government is a government in favour of cheap food for the working people. I have a case in my constituency where it means all the difference between expanded operation and contracted operation

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
if the sales tax is removed or if it is kept . on. That may seem like a minor matter, but it is interesting and instructive as one of the examples of the want of consideration that has been given by this wonderful government in the preparation of these wonderful budget changes.
I want to pass for a moment to something that, I think, is of more importance than a special instance. I am impressed with the idea that matters are not being grappled with on a big enough and broad enough scale in this country. These tariff alterations are at best a mere haphazard, piffling bit of work. Other countries of the world that are solvent since the war are dev.oting their energies to an actual reduction of their debt We are disputing in this House whether you ought to enter a certain set of figures in one book or in another, or put them on one page or another, and we know that we are not reducing our real liabilities. In the same way we come to this House and discuss a question whether you can stand a rate of 5 cents, or 7i cents, or 10 cents, on some particular commodities. What is pressing down upon internal business in this country to-day? The sales tax as amplified by the present government, this government that was going to abolish oppressive taxes. What did the United States do after the Civil War? Within a comparatively few years, as soon as they pulled their country together, the first thing they did was, not to lower their external tariff walls, but to remove the things that were burdensome upon the internal commerce of the country. I ask: Why, instead of taking a few cents off here and a few cents off there in the protective tariff, if this government had 824,000,000 of tariff they felt they could reduce, why did they not take the whole $24,000,000 off their sales tax, give the people real and vital relief, and let the tariff stay as it was, good enough for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) last year and'good enough for many of his Liberal predecessors? The farmers themselves, the agricultural interests that are represented here, tell the government plainly and frankly that they do not think this reduction amounts to very much to them. Some of them say that, after all, the question of the West is not a question of tariff. Many members in the House to my left have said that, and yet the government, in the hope of and for the sake of political support, carries an unwanted gift to the provinces of the West, where it might distribute its favours, if it has favours to give, or its benefits, if it has
benefits to bestow, on all the people of Canada from the Pacific to the Atlantic. But we find an outpouring about the unity of Canada and the West and the East being brought together and all that sort of stuff. The East and the West can and will get together, but it will be upon the principle of equal opportunity and equal sacrifice to the needs of the nation, and not by patting a special portion oh the back as long as it votes right.
I do not want to take up more time to-night but as the tariff has been discussed at considerable length, I am going to pay a few minutes' attention to something of the history of tariff issues. I am not going to read what some professor has written in a textbook of theory; but I propose to turn to solutions of facts, some of them in this country and some of them in the next best available instance, in the country lying to the south of us. I believe it is better to proceed by building upon the actual accumulated knowledge of the past than to base your policies upon mere conjectures and hopes for the present. If you will go back in our own country as far as 1855 you will find that there was a period of great prosperity in Canada caused largely by the building of the Grand Trunk railway. There was at that time a tremendous expansion and a very great land boom was on. In 1857 the boom collapsed and Canada was in a state of crisis. In 1858, as a remedy for conditions of that character, Sir Alexander Galt first introduced the protective principle into the tariff of Canada. It was successful and industry sprang up. I have neither the time nor the inclination to-night to go into statistics; I want to weary the audience as little as possible. But I propose to put the facts on record, because I believe they are of value not merely historically but practically as well. In 1866 because of the impending confederation Canada reduced the tariff to an average of 15 per cent; the Maritime provinces' average at that time was 12 1-2 per cent. Canada during that period had been greatly helped by the condition of the United States. Immediately after the Civil War in the United States there was an absolute paralysis of industry and there was a high internal taxation which continued down to about 1873,1 think. Those conditions afforded a virtual protection to the people of Canada; but in 1873 the United States, recovering from their war burdens, reducing internal taxation, came into competition with us in our own lowly protected markets. I am not going to discuss whether we had a tariff for revenue or for protection in Canada; I will simply say
The Budget-Mr. Baxter

that we had a tariff low enough for the American manufacturer to get over the barrier and sell to our own people in the market which should have been our own. What happened? The Liberal party was in charge of affairs at that time in 1873; Sir Richard Cart-wright was its great exponent. I will give you a few words from a public utterance of his in parliament. He said:
It becomes us to consider the various remedies proposed for this unfortunate state of affairs.
In the first place I desire to expend a few words on the general impression which prevails, even in quarters where we would hardly expect to find it, that it is in the power of this government, of any government, this legislature or any legislature to make the country prosperous by the mere stroke of a pen or the enactment of acts of parliament. I would like hon. gentlemen in this House and out of it, who entertain that illusion, as I consider it, to think to what such a course would lead and would ask them if they are prepared to pay the price. You cannot have at one and the same time a free government and a paternal government.
His solution was no solution at all. From 1873 to 1878, as we know, Canada passed through one of the worst periods in her history, and it was only by the advent of the Conservative party to power with Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Charles Tupper, Sir Leonard Tilley and Sir George Etienne Cartier, at the head of affairs, that a real National Policy was introduced which preserved to this country its own markets and its own industries. And it is only in so far as that beneficent policy has not been completely expunged from the statutes of Canada that Canada has been able to succeed in the years which have followed the Conservative administration. The United States had precisely the same experience. From 1818 to 1824 they had what hon. gentlemen would call a revenue tariff. The balance of trade was against them, and in that period exports of specie itself exceeded imports by over $10,000,000. In 1824 they adopted the protective tariff and the results were immediately gratifying, so much so that in 1828 they passed a higher tariff and enjoyed a period of unequalled prosperity down to 1834. In that period they imported $30,000,000 more of specie than they exported and paid off the debt incurred during the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812. But there was too much prosperity; then came that phrase which has become so familiar in these days, "a step in the right direction." A step in the right direction was taken, no doubt amidst as great plaudits as it has received to-day. The tariff was lowered to 20 per cent, a higher average tariff than we have to-day and meaning a great deal more in those days of nearly a century ago. They tinkered with the tariff,

they lowered it, and in a very few years the government, as a writer put it, was out of funds and credit. So serious was the situation that^ in 1842 they went back to protection and again they experienced a period of prosperity. Once more, however, another "step in the right direction" was taken with a new tariff in 1846 and that was followed by an absolute crash. There may be other causes, but I call the attention of hon. members to the fact that every time they took that step in the right direction, every time they lowered the tariff, they were invaded by foreign manufacturers and a financial crash ensued, in that country which was then in a process of building itself up comparable to Canada at the present time.
Experience teaches, they say, but I have yet to learn that it teaches a Liberal government. Now, let us have an example that occurred in this country in 1872. At, that time the United States government took the duty off tea and Canada followed suit; but when she did she found a clause in the United States law by which a duty of 10 per cent was charged on all tea imported from countries west of the Cape of Good Hope-a sort of jigger in it such as we should get if we went into reciprocity with the United States. Ten per cent was exacted on all tea imported into the United States from Canada; so that while we had free trade in tea with the United States they had protection against us. This is the same policy as the Progressive government is pursuing to-day step by step and adopted by its liberal junta. Canada at that time took to itself power to impose a duty of 10 per cent on all tea coming from the United States, an equivalent of the duty imposed by the United States on that commodity going from Canada; and the trade was saved until in 1874 our Liberal friends, with Sir Richard Cartwright as Minister of Finance, took hold of the helm again, when they succeeded in very short order in ruining the tea trade. Then the tea dealers went to the United States and sent circulars into this market inviting the people to purchase tea on the other side of the line. Our direct trade was gone, a fine accomplishment, one apparently so fine that the greatest ambition of the Prime Minister and his colleagues to-day is to have it repeated in an almost infinitely larger number of articles than the government of that time dealt with.
This question of protection has been discussed to-night in very measured terms and very fairly by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), but if you follow his remarks to their logical conclusion what be-

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
comes of Canada? Have we a cohesive country? You have, if you are prepared to make Canada one vast agricultural tract from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I speak from the standpoint of the Maritime provinces, and I have just as good a right to speak from that standpoint as other hon. gentlemen have to speak from the standpoint of other sections of the country. It is only by this common discussion in parliament of the difficulties with which we are confronted in different parts of the Dominion that we will be able to evolve any policy which will do reasonable justice towards all parts. I would put the situation of the Maritimes in this way: You take the duties down low enough, you let our protection fail us, and you soon reach the point at which our very mines will cease to operate because the United States can produce more cheaply and can use us for a dumping market. I am supported in that by the statements that have been made by hon. members behind the government. There is no question between us. Now, if you protect the development of our natural products in steel and in coal, you increase the population in certain centres. The moment you increase that population the demand comes upon the rural districts to provide food for that population. It is the old story of the home market. It ought not to be necessary to discuss it in this year 1924, but apparently it is necessary to re-state the fundamental principles all over again.
Our position is different from that of the West. The man in the West who is mining wheat instead of coal has to compete in the world market. We cannot help him except in one way, as I see it: we can find him the cheapest transportation that the country can afford to give him. That is infinitely more valuable to him than a few dollars off his farm implements. We in the East are prepared to make sacrifices, and we have made sacrifices, for that very thing. The Canadian Pacific railway was built out of sacrifices of the older provinces.
Oh, no.
Oh, yes. The newer provinces did not build the Canadian Pacific railway.
A lot of our land out there paid for it.
The land was bought and paid for by the older provinces.
We are paying for it.

It was Canada's gift, it was part of the price of getting the railway built. And it made settlement possible. We do not begrudge it, and we do not want to
go back on it. But I ask: As we made the development of the West possible, is it not fair'that the West should in some way make possible the development of the natural resources of the East? Let us look where we stand to-day. I am not going to discuss in a spirit of asperity what has taken place with regard to the Crowsnest pass agreement. I just refer to the fact that that agreement was made not between the provinces at all; it was a rider put by Canada upon the assistance given to the Crowsnest Pass railway. The western people get the benefit of that to-day.
If that agreement had never been made what possible argument would the West have against the equality of freight rates all over the Dominion? Do they not realize that the very fact that they enjoy the rates under that agreement-whether rightly or wrongly we need not discuss now-means that the people in other parts of Canada and in regard to other commodities have to pay more than they otherwise would? That is the burden we are bearing daily and hourly in other parts of the Dominion. Is it too much for us to ask that our gateways-in the East, Quebec and Montreal in the summer, our gateway in the West, Vancouver, all the year around, and our gateways in the Maritimes, Halifax and St. John, in the winter, shall be used by the western people in preference to searching for a special route for their freight by the j gateways of the neighbouring nation? I say frankly, you cannot expect this to go on all the time if there is to be a Canada for us, so long as our income tax is to be paid and our sales tax and our customs dues to maintain our railways and to build further extensions in the West. We are not begrudging that expenditure, but we cannot have the West say: There is no Canada east of the Great Lakes or east of Quebec. We say we want our share in the handling of this western produce. That is the case of the Maritime provinces on transportation. And do not think for a moment that we are going to relieve the situation by getting out of confederation, or even talking about getting out of it. We are going to stay in confederation, and we are proud to be in it. But we are going to keep everlastingly at this question until we make the same impression upon the country and upon parliament as our western friends have made in regard to some other matters. They have shown us the benefit of agitation, and we are going to do the agitating. I believe that my own party tonight stands back of the reasonable requests of the Maritime provinces. If I thought otherwise I would mighty soon part company with it.
The Budget-Mr. Baxter
Oh, oh.

Hon. members laugh.. I will go a step further for them. After the next election comes there will be another government. I might, perhaps not unreasonably, expect to be included in that government, but I would not enter it unless I were sure that I would get justice for the Maritime provinces.
Does my hon. friend mean the portfolio of Justice?

I would tell my hon. friends that there are people who could fill it worse. I am not at all conceited, for I can be fair, but I have met some people who cannot be. I want to pursue for a moment the statement I started to make-if I found after assuming office that I had been mistaken in my party, I would leave the seats of the mighty and go into such opposition as there was opportunity to consort with. That is the difference between the attitude that I consider must be taken in order for the Maritime provinces to be successful in their fight for their rights and the attitude that has been persistently and consistently taken by the "solid sixteen" as they were in this House. One of those hon. gentlemen has taken office at the hands of the government, and a very effective stopper has been put in his mouth as far as any advocacy of the rights of the Maritime provinces is concerned. We have heard no motion for a duty on coal nor for a duty on steel, we have heard no motion to take the duty off flour-none of these things that he promised his constituents. We have heard protests from the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), and when he got away from his free trade heresy I have agreed with the other things he has said. But does the hon. member realize how utterly helpless he has been? During one admirable speech he made I, a poor, miserable, benighted Conservative, had to appeal to the Speaker to preserve order among his friends so that we on this side could hear him. That is the sympathy the Maritime provinces have got from the Liberal party, that is the sympathy the hon. member for Cumberland has received from his party in doing his duty by standing up for the rights of his native province. I have not heard any other members from Nova Scotia trying to do what he did. What they should have done was to have said to their leaders: We are a solid sixteen. We are Liberals. We have followed you. We have borne the heat and burden of the day. You are now on the eve of making a trade with the western provinces for political support. If you make that

trade for the sake of that support, you are going to lose the stalwart friends you have had in the past unless you give an even square deal to the part of the country we represent.
My hon. friends of those sixteen were sup- [DOT] porting the right hon. the Prime Minister when he was in the depths of opposition. They went to the country asking the country to get back of him. They were not like people to my left who went to the country saying they had no faith in the present Prime Minister and no faith in his party. And yet it is far, far more unequal than the story of the Prodigal Son. These people who were never in the fold have had everything heaped upon them. The faithful sons who stayed at home, who would not raise a voice of protest, have seen the fatted calf killed and the table spread for the benefit of those who had been, if not spending their substance in riotous living, at least not been living at home within the ambit of the Liberal party.
I want to say a word about this coal business from the standpoint of Nova Scotia. Now my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) advocated a greater duty. He said: "Let us make this Dominion one; you people in Ontario burn our coal." Well, what have we heard in parliament? All sorts of devices, and a committee sitting day after day and week after week to see if it is possible for the Canadian National Railways to bring lignite from some part of Alberta into Toronto, when the best coal in the world was hundreds of miles nearer, accessible most of the year by water, all the year by rail, and nobody ever raised a voice of protest or demanded that the rates on the railway should be made low enough to give Nova Scotia coal the entrance into the markets of upper Canada that were promised to it on every platform when confederation was discussed.

with Sir Henry Thornton, from what I have sometimes noticed people choosing in regard to speeches they have made. I pursued a course which commended itself to my judgment, a course which, I think, met with the approval of Sir Henry Thornton as a gentleman. This is what I said to him:
I did refer to you as "an imported miracle" because, as I explained to the audience, that is the way the government press treats you. I did say that you were born in the United States and that you subsequently went to England. That was said in explanation of the fact that you had little or no experience of local conditions and that you had been given a board to advise you, many of whose members were mere political hacks who would be of no assistance to you except along certain political lines.
I did not say that you were "knighted for some pretended service."
I read this part of the letter in order to do justice to Sir Henry Thornton, because the newspaper report of my speech certainly did him an injustice, and it is only right that I should take an occasion as public as this, not of making reparation for my own fault, but of relieving him from the annoyance that must have been caused by what I contend was an inaccurate report. This is what I said to him:
I have talked to the reporter who wrote the article and he says that his recollection is that I did say it. Nevertheless I am positive that I did not. All I know about your knighthood and all that I need to know about it is that it was given for war service and nothing could be farther from my thoughts or expression than to refer to these services as pretended.
You will notice that even if a thing makes against me I do not go back on it.
The reporter, who is a conscientious hardworking chap with a desire to be absolutely accurate, admits that he may not have accurately expressed my statement when he used the words, " thrown out of a job in England." He admits that that reads as if you had been ignominiously dismissed and that I did not use language to convey that impression but merely referred to the cessation of your employment there. I did also refer to men having been removed as, " the second deportation of the Aeadians."
While from my own explanation you may think that the report is a fairly accurate one, yet I can frankly say that it does not in my judgment fairly reflect the character of my address. If you own a lot of land, and your neighbour owns a lot of land adjoining, that neighbour can pass over any part of his land when he likes and you have nothing to say about it. If, however, you buy his land you can stop him from even putting a foot upon it. I do not think we can get any political difference on that statement; the political difference comes when we talk about a railway running to a Maritime port or to Portland, Maine. So long as the Grand Trunk Railway Company, a private company organized and financed by British capital, owned the Grand Trunk railway, which had one of its connections running from Montreal to Portland, Maine, the people of Canada had no fair right to say to the private owners of that road: You shall not carry traffic over the lines of steel that you have laid down out of your own pocket. The moment the people of Canada bought that road and took it over they had as good a right to stop the use of those rails as they had to stop the use of any other part of the system. My question is:	Why do
they not do it?

I would ask my hon. friend
if he thinks that the government of this country to-day, after the late administration
TMr. Baxter. 1
under the right hon. leader of the opposition took the good money of Canada to buy the Grand Trunk from Montreal to Portland, should tear up the rails, abandon that portion of the road, and throw into the Atlantic ocean the money that was so improvidently spent by the late administration.

I wonder my hon. friend
had not asked his question long ago. My complete answer is:	They slashed a way
through the province of New Brunswick, and ran what was once the National Transcontinental from Grand Falls to Moncton, with the idea of helping Nova Scotia-and it has never helped Nova Scotia one five-cent piece.
That is not an answer.

I cannot give an answer
all in one sentence. My hon. friend took three hours and forty minutes the. other night, and now he will have to give me some time. Now, on the National Transcontinental the rails are fairly rusty. It develops no local business. It does not help the province of Nova Scotia. The present government, or its political board, is not making daily use of those rails. Now, may I ask my hon. friend if the National Railway Board is bound to use those rails every day because they belong to the government?
My hon. friend-

Wait a minute. That did not come because of anything that my leader or any government he was associated with did; that came because of the unfortunate arrangement which was made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding. But the country has got the road just the same. It is a curse upon the country, but I do not see that that is any reason why we should waste money running trains over it every day if there is not business to warrant such operation. I would suggest that as we have not got traffic enough to run over that road and to run down to Portland at the same time, we should simply take the traffic that goes down to Portland and route it over those other rails into the ports of Halifax and St. John, using the rails within our own country. Now, of those two great connections one is bound to lie idle and unproductive. Shall the unproductive road be within Canada and the productive road in the United States? Or is this House and the present government willing to reverse the position? I understand Sir Henry Thornton, according to the newspapers, says that his business is to make money out of the whole system, and he is going to do it. Therefore until the government gives him directions to the contrary he

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
will be perfectly right in following that course. That means that where he can make more money by routing traffic through United States Atlantic ports than through Canadian Atlantic ports, then under his present declaration Sir Henry Thornton will route it to the American ports. What I want as compensation for what we in the Maritime provinces have given up and for what we are suffering is the mandate of the people of Canada, expressed through this government, to Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors: Here, even if you make less money by handling the traffic through Canadian ports, that is the way you must route it, and that is the National railway policy of Canada.
If shippers in Canada will not route their traffic except through Portland, how are you going to make Sir Henry Thornton do as you propose?

In the first place, my hon. friend is beguiled by this myth of routing. There is not nearly so much specific routing as he thinks or as we are led to believe. In the second place, my hon. friend ought to know painfully that back in 1898 a Liberal government put a differential on the Intercolonial railway against the port of Halifax and in favour of the port of St. John, and that that was removed only a few months ago.
That was agreed to by the people of Halifax and by the Board of Trade of Halifax.
And it was complained of, and justly so, ever afterwards.
It was done under statute.
Surely my hon. friend has had experience enough of the power of a differential.
Oh yes.

And if Sir Henry Thornton wants to serve Canadian ports, all he has to do is to charge a higher rate-which is a differential-for hauling to Portland, Maine, than to Halifax or St. John, and the freight will go by the cheaper route.

Does my hon. friend realize that as soon as the traffic gets into the United States it is subject to the Interstate Commerce Commission? I am treading on delicate ground. Let the Canadian National Railway take steps towards making traffic in the United States difficult over the line that we own in that country, and he will find where we will land with the Canadian National, not in the East but in the West where we get our through traffic.
13Si
There is a way of dealing with that-make your rates cheaper to St. John and Halifax, and let the country bear the difference for the sake of building up the National railway.
That is another policy.
Oh, oh.

I hear groans. There is to be no Canadian national spirit for the benefit of the Maritime provinces, but we can submit to the Crowsnest pass agreement for the benefit of another part of Canada. Is that the way to bring east and west together? Is that making a United Canada? Where are all the Prime Minister's platitudes now, in view of the groans and roars from the other side of the House-platitudes about Canadian unity denied and discarded by his own followers almost before his voice had ceased to echo in this room. Let us come right out in the open and see where we stand. We will find out whether it is to be a united Canada, or whether it is to be united without us. As I said before, you will not drive us out of Confederation, but you are starting now the agitation on the part of the Maritime provinces that will eventually win this case, and you may as well prepare yourselves to adjust the business of the country to those conditions, for sooner or later you will have to do it.
The hon. gentleman started that propaganda last fall.

I did not start that propaganda last fall. I started the idea of Maritime unity long before, and I have joined in with the idea of Maritime co-operation, but what I found was that in the city of Halifax, and I think throughout the province of Nova Scotia, the idea is there among the people and it will get expression. I have been one of those who gave it voice, and only one among a number, but the feeling is so deep-rooted that the government is going to realize what the real soul of Nova Scotia is feeling over the treatment it has received.
Now I call the attention of the House to another fact. Out of the ports of Canada to the United Kingdom and to other countries, wheat and flour, all converted into terms of bushels, were exported in 1922 to the amount of 61,000,000 bushels, and by United States ports in the same year over 113,000,000 bushels; in 1923 nearly 116,000,000 bushels were exported through Canadian ports, and nearly 149,000,000 bushels through United States ports, a better relative showing. But the object of our railways should be to in-
The Budget-Mr. Baxter

duce the export of every bushel of Canadian wheat through Canadian ports. I am not asking now for any special privilege for the Maritime provinces. I am only asking the Liberal party to be true to its really great leader, to implement the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who said he would never be satisfied until every pound of Canadian traffic was carried over Canadian rails to Canadian ports.

He never intended to buy
the Grand Trunk then.

But he intended to build
the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental, and he built them.
All in Canada.

Certainly, all in Canada.
I wonder if my hon. friend objects to taking traffic from Ontario or other parts over the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Certainly not.

I would hope not. I wonder if my hon. friend realizes that the traffic would be comparatively small if it were limited to traffic originating on the Transcontinental railway, and not very large if it were limited to the Grand Trunk Pacific. The real feeders have been the portions of the Canadian National system, and without them this system of railroads would not have had much vitality. .Personally I would rather have seen it under private management, but it is now under public management, and I want that management directed to make the best use of the road for Canadian ports on the Pacific and on the Atlantic.
Now on this transportation question someone spoke at a public meeting in the interests of the Liberal party in tolerably similar language to what I am about to utter:
Would you consider that it is wise to send these people back? In the old days we could send coal in the winter time from the mines at Stellarton to Montreal. The freight rates under the Liberal government were $1.90 a ton return for nearly a thousand miles. The rate that Colonel Cantley and D. B. Hanna have to-day is $1.20, or an increase of $2.30 per ton on Nova Scotia coal when you send it to Montreal.
Take steel. What was the rate charged on steel in the days of the Liberal government? Cost from Trenton to Montreal $3.50 per ton. What is the rate to-day-$7.80 per ton, an increase of $4.30 a ton on steel. Is it any wonder that the steel works are not working?
But we who are fighting the battles of the Liberal party are pledged to at once take steps to see that the I.C.R. comes back to the hands of the people of the Maritime provinces and that it will be operated under a readjustment of the freight rates, where only the cost of operation of the part of the railway in which we are interested will have to be taken into account.
I Mr. Baxter.]
Well, I wonder if anybody ever made that promise. I wonder if any member from Nova Scotia has ever attempted to implement it. I wait for an answer.
Let me point out to the House some of what might be called minor matters in railway rates that do not receive the adjustment or the attention I think they should in the Maritime provinces. The other night the hon. member for Prince represented me as having somewhat improperly dealt with certain railway rates. Now I dealt with the reductions according to the best information I could get, and I know the figures are substantially correct. I would ask the hon. member to compare the rates of 1897 all over Canada with those of 1924, and he will find that our rates in the Maritime provinces, and generally the rest of Canada are vastly higher, that the rates shot up for a few years while the Crowsnest pass agreement was suspended, and they are now back again to the terms of that agreement. There was some little alteration by the Railway Commission, but, very small, and I think a moment's comparison of the rates as they are now with the rates for the same products in 1897 will convince the member for Prince that there is something that calls for his work in trying to get a re-adjustment, instead of simply petty criticism of the addresses that have been delivered against the government in the by-election in Halifax.
I have in my possession a letter from the Mann Axe Company of St. Stephen, NJB., and it throws rather an illuminating light on the treatment the railway accords to manufacturers. Now we have basic materials in Nova Scotia, and we are willing to manufacture in New Brunswick. We want our market, and what treatment do we get? The Mann Axe Company say in December last:
We ordered some goods from Brockville for expoifc to Newfoundland, freight was to be allowed to North Sydney, but instead of any freight allowance we have a charge of the difference between 75c. and 97c. per 100 lbs.
And they go on to quote the railway's confirmation :
As the rate from Brockville to North Sydney is 75c. per 100 lbs. and the rate from St. Stephen to North Sydney is 97c. per 100 lbs., you can readily understand there is no freight allowance to be given you, but instead a charge of 22c. per 100 lbs.
These people are to-day the only manufacturers in their line of any consequence in the Maritime provinces. Two other concerns have been driven out of business in St. John, probably on account of freight rates, companies that had been manufacturing for nearly

The Budget-Mr. Baxter
fifty years. Now instead of manufacturing axes in St. John one of the concerns is importing from the upper provinces goods they are selling under their own brand and label.
That is not the sort of thing that conduces to a satisfactory industrial condition.
Which firm is doing that?
I think it is the Campbell Brothers that are doing it.
Not the Mann Axe Company?

No. This other company
went out of business as far as manufacturing is concerned.

When did they go out
of business?
The Mann Axe Company is not out of business; it is this other concern.
When did they go out?

Just a few years ago.
That is they went out of the business of manufacturing. They are selling articles made elsewhere.

I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend but I am very sensitive as to complaints about our railways being unfair. The complaint as read by the Mann Axe Company is based on a statement by them that they were promised a certain rate and did not get.it. Now where is the proof that they were promised such a rate?

I cannot say, that, but
what I point out is this: Instead of having oppressive local rates in handling business of this character they should be given the benefit of some kind of a through rate to Newfoundland, an export rate. Now I am told the same thing comes up in regard to Newfoundland which depends largely upon the Maritime provinces for some imported commodities, among them fodder for live stock. In 1922 New Brunswick had a good crop of hay. But the furtherance charge on this commodity via North Sydney was withdrawn leaving regular local mileage rates on hay in effect. In consequence New Brunswick could not compete. Now, Newfoundland purchases largely in the United States. Commodities arriving from Chicago and Central Association points are covered by tariffs granting furtherance rates to North Sydney and thus compete with Canadian manufacturers. In other words people running from Chicago points can get these furtherance rates and people in Canada and the eastern part of Canada do not get them.
Then we have in regard to Prince Edward Island a special commodity tariff on oats in carload lots. I am told this is merely a farce, and that the so-called special rates that were put on from points in Prince Edward Island to Maritime provinces points for local deliveries were nothing better than standard 8 class rates.
Then we have on examination of the tariff the undoubted fact that on iron and steel commodities from 1916 to the present date rates have been advanced from 100 to 150 per cent. From the government of my own province which professes to be dealing with the matter of freight rates I find there has not been a single representation made here on the subject of railway rates. At any rate in a return brought down to the House I looked in vain for any communication from them. I do not know what they are doing. Up to a few weeks ago there had not been a single letter, or telegram, or bit of correspondence produced. I think the railway authorities ought to be alive to the situation but I am rather surprised that the provincial government of New Brunswick would be so supine in this matter when there has been so much discussion in the Legislative Assembly with regard to it.
Now I want to come to something else. I know this speech is painfully long, but there are not many opportunities of bringing some of these matters to the attention of parliament. I have been discussing railway problems from what I think is largely a local standpoint. There is a bigger standpoint than that. I tried to emphasize earlier in my address the necessity for tackling as big a thing as the sales tax and eliminating it as soon as possible. There is a similar proposition to be grappled with in connection with the railway and yet it does not seem to matter as no one thinks of it. Do hon. members realize that the operating revenue from all the railways of Canada aggregates nearly $475,000,000. That is not merely the Canadian Pacific and the National but takes in all the smaller roads. That in other words is the total amount of money that the people of Canada as a whole pay for railway rates whether passenger or freight. Now that is distributed among several roads but the principal earners of the money are the National and the Canadian Pacific; the others are almost negligible. Now what do we see going on in the country from day to day? These two great national systems-for they are both national-jockeying one another for position. Almost any day that you went into the railway committee room lately you would find some discussion about possible parallels. An
The Budget-Mr. Baxter

examination of the railway map shows the parallel. All you have got to do is to take a trip, for instance, from Ottawa to Montreal and you find practically four parallels. Go from Montreal to Toronto and you have parallels. There are many other parts of the Dominion where you will find parallels. The whole administration of both railways to-day is based on the principle of competition. People say when there is competition the consumer gets the benefit. In this case the rates are fixed by the railway commission and all that this competition can do is to increase the cost of service. I had the honour of suggesting that idea to the former Minister of Railways, Hon. Mr. Kennedy, and I wish to say again, as I said before, that I regret very much that death put an untimely end to his career, because I believe he was a man big enough and strong enough to have grappled with this railway problem. I trust that my hon. friend who occupies the position of Minister of Railways at the present time may have vigor enough and interest enough to grapple with the problem as well.
On a question as large as this is I think it is my duty as well as my privilege to give suggestions. My suggestion is this:	I think
these two roads ought to be asked not to compete but to co-operate. I would suggest that the directorate of each should appoint some small committee that would have no power whatever except -the power of consultation and making representations, and that that joint committee should, with all the expert advice possible, devote itself to the problem of settling what service or forms of service can be dispensed with in Canada, still preserving to the people, not perhaps the service that they want nor perhaps the service that they think they are [DOT]willing to pay for but the service they ought to be able to afford to pay for. There are many places in Canada where we do not need palatial trains or palatial cars. Where two points are connected all the special services could go by one line. If one road gets it the other road may feel it is not being treated fairly, but that can be compensated for by giving it something in another part of the country. In other words put the two of them together to solve the problem as if it were one of joint operation. What will the result be? That their operating expenses will decline and that by the decline of the operating expenses the demands on the people of Canada, who foot the total of this bill of $475,000,000, will be lessened. The money that is returned to the pockets of the people for railway service is just as much a remission of taxation as the money that is cut off by lower duties on any particular commodity.

Now there, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker and gentlemen, is a real problem and one of enough magnitude to be worth tackling. This is no piffling about five per cent or two and a half per cent or anything of that kind- not a discussion between a lawn mower and a reaper. It is a big thing. It may easily mean $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 saved to the people of Canada, or $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 more left in the common pot to be available to bear the burden of the country. That is the real economy that is worth considering, not the sort of economy that roots among the offices of the Civil Service and tries to cut off $400 here and $500 there, and winds up by saving $30,000 or $40,000. I do not say that should not be done, if useless or unnecessary people are being employed, but all you can save by those methods is a mere nothing. Tackle a big problem when you are at it and go at it man fashion.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister in an address to this House said the only questions that were discussed in the by-elections of Kent and Halifax were local questions, except where appeals were made as they had been made by the hon. member for St. John of a sectional character-sectional appeals to one part of the country setting it over against the other. He also added that among the government following from one end of the country to the other, the fact that many of those who had been bitterly opposed to the government, men who had been prominent in Tory circles had been given political appointments under civil service administration, more than anything else had created dissatisfaction with the government. The Prime Minister is quite right that there is dissatisfaction with the government from one end of the country to the other, but he is entirely mistaken as to the cause. He may repudiate the Civil Service Commission if he will, but he has not pricked the blister yet.
If what I have said to-night be sectional, if it be unpatriotic, or if it be putting one class against another, or one part of the country against the other, I tell him that this is precisely the sort of talk that I and others associated with me indulged in in the counties of Halifax and Kent, and that we found a body of people there who needed no preparation, who were thinking the same thing and only asking public men to give expression to it, and yet I have heard the attitude we have adopted described by some hon. members in this House as parochial; and it seems to me that it comes to this: If you talk about spending the public money to bring coal at less than cost from Alberta

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
to Ottawa then it is national. If you speak of bringing coal at cost from Cumberland to Montreal, it is parochial. If you speak of carrying wheat, lumber or fish from the Pacific, it is national. If the concessions apparently are all to be for one interest, then it is national, to the deprivation of all other interests. If we complain about it, we are parochial. Free trade evidently is national in its scope, protection apparently is parochial. Tell that sort of thing to the artisans of this country who depend upon that protection, and who depend upon a wise and fair solution of our transportation problems in order to enable them to participate to the fullest extent that this country can afford. In conclusion I ask this House and this country to adopt a real policy, give us Canadian railways for Canadian ports. Give us a limitation of the British preference to British bottoms and to Canadian ports, give us Canadian tariff to protect Canadian interests, give us Canadian coal for the use of Canadian people, give us Canadian steel for Canadian use, enable us to transport Canadian fish to Canadian consumers. In short, let us have Canadian products for Canadian users and Canadian railways for the Canadian people - national policy from beginning to end and from East to West.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must apologize, Mr. Speaker, for attempting to address the House at this late hour. I am not responsible, however, for the lateness of the hour. My hon. friend who preceded me is more responsible than I am. I will omit the usual preliminary remarks and the usual compliments. I will try to deal with the questions before the House from a national viewpoint and not from the point of view of an election campaign in the Maritime provinces. The budget is a Liberal budget. That is why my hon, friend seems to dislike it. It is based on the traditional policy of the Liberal party, a policy which is one not of free trade but of freer trade, and based on a proper consideration of the interests of all classes of the community. It has been greeted with satisfaction by the large majority of the people of Canada. It will carry much larger support when the clouds of poison gas that have been spread are lifted, and when the troops of bogeys who have been let loose to play havoc with the common sense and intelligence of the population are dissipated.
The government has redeemed the pledge that was given in the Speech from the Throne. Three or four days before the budget was delivered, I believe, the right hon. leader of
the opposition (Mr. Meighen) addressed a meeting in the city of Windsor, and ventured a prediction that there would be no reduction in the duties on implements of production. As usual he was wrong. My only hope is that experience will teach him the wisdom of some modesty in political predictions. The government has redeemed its pledge, has reduced taxation by an amount of $24,000,000, and has removed that burden from the shoulders of the ratepayers of Canada. It is rather a large amount. Three dollars per head for every man, woman and child in Canada might seem a very small sum for the financial magnates of the opposition, but it is quite an amount for the hardworking labouring men and the farmers, and that reduction has been made on articles which have been used by the many rather than the few .
I have heard some members in this House express regret that the income tax has not been reduced. My hon. friend from Waterloo (Mr. Elliott) is one of those who expressed that regret. The payment of taxes by itself in an irksome task. The rendering of returns to the government puts one in an ill frame of mind. Even I, with my serene and calm temper, must confess that I am not exempt from that weakness, but the income tax has that advantage of being levied on those who are more able to pay it.. Before the income tax could be reduced, the burden of taxation should be lessened on those of the poorer classes of the community.
In dealing with the budget and more particularly with the changes in our taxation, the government had to take into account three main considerations; the necessities of the revenue, the needs of industry and the interests of consumers. I have already stated in this House that I am not a fanatic in matters of trade. The words "protection" and "free trade" are not to me the red rag which they seem to be to some of my friends on both sides of the controversy. This is a very imperfect world, and we have to deal with things as they are rather than as we wish them to be. A battle of words or on words is useless. The word "protection" in itself is a fine word and it appeals to me; but I would rather like its meaning to be broader, and I would apply it to the farmer, the labourer and the consumer at large, and protect them against high prices of articles which they have to buy.
I have met few people who do not admit that a condition under which nations would exchange the articles which they are best able
.2180
The Budget-Mr. Lapointe

to produce would be a beneficial condition to everybody. Most protectionists admit that, but they dismiss this statement at once as an ideal which cannot be attained. The discussion in the House on this budget has shown the accuracy of my statement. I have heard the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) defend protection or a tariff as a bargaining power with other countries. Bargaining for what? Bargaining, indeed, to obtain concessions and to haye larger freedom of exchange with that country. I have heard the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) defend protection and claim that the tariff was necessary as a weapon for retaliation. What is the purpose of retaliation, if not to obtain concessions from the country against which retaliation is made? Indeed, those were the arguments of Mr. Chamberlain when he launched his campaign in England for tariff reform, and in Canada that was the great argument of the father of the so-called National Policy in 1878. He made it a part of his resolution in the Canadian House of Commons when he introduced the National Policy in this country. These are the last words of his resolution:
And moving-as it ought to do-in the direction of a reciprocity of tariffs with our neighbours, so far as the varied interests of Canada may demand, will greatly tend to procure for this country, eventually, a reciprocity of trade.
The idea of a greater freedom of trade should not, therefore, be abhorrent to any of those hon. gentlemen who admit that their policy or doctrine is temporary, is not an end, but a means, and should end when the goal is reached which they intend to reach. That is a reason why there cannot be any permanency of tariff, because when the bargaining power which the hon. member for Centre Vancouver spoke of is used successfully and when the retaliation suggested by the hon. member for Kingston is also used successfully,	in order to secure better
and longer freedom of trade with other countries, then obviously the goal is reached and there must be a change in our tariff. Only in freedom could stability be made permanent, and we all think that it is impossible to have free trade in this country at the present time.
As regards stability, did you notice, Mr. Speaker, that those who proclaim most loudly the necessity of stability are quite willing to compromise when the demand is for an increase of duty? Stability works when the question is one of reduction, but the principles are not quite so inflexible when there is a demand for higher duties. I cannot admire I Mr. Lapointe.]
such logic and consistency. If reciprocity is admittedly the goal of many protectionists, I believe that a common ground could be found. There are few free trade doctrinaires in this country. Most people who oppose protection do not like the artificial raising of prices on many articles at the expense of the community; but they admit, as a rule, that the tariff is a means of getting revenue, and as there must be revenue in Canada, especially at the present time, in order to meet the expenditure of the country, there could not be any great objection to a tariff for the purpose of securing that revenue. High protection as well as free trade would kill the revenue. When the protection is so high that the foreign goods cannot enter this country, there is no customs duty, no revenue, and other forms of taxation must be devised. Those duties, if applied scientifically from a business viewpoint, in such a way as not to hamper production in those basic and indigenous industries of our country, will still afford an incidental protection	that should	be
sufficient to preserve our industries. Is not then a tariff for revenue a basis on which well meaning, reasonable moderate people could have an understanding? Is not a tariff for revenue a fair compromise? Compromise, after all, in the sense of avoiding extremes, is a British characteristic; the British Empire has been built on compromise, and by compromise it has been kept alive. My hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) the other day said that we were opportunists on this side of the House. I remember having read a speech of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman in answer to a similar charge made against him in the British House of Commons, and he said virtually this: "Well, there is such a thing as good opportunism in the sense of not endeavouring to do what is at the moment impossible and not rushing precipitately at the thing which cannot be attained immediately; for in trying so to accomplish your purpose you are apt to hurt the very cause which it is your desire to serve." That, I agree, is good opportunism. Why, Mr. Speaker, most of the good that is accomplished in the world is accomplished by such means. Every soldier that knows his business is an opportunist; every seaman battling with the elements is an opportunist; so is every physician and every engineer. Even St. Paul was an opportunist, because he said:
All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient.	.
In economic as well as in other spheres the part of wisdom is to avoid extreme views,

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
to eschew the too much and the too little, the too fast and the too slow, and even to be capable of retracing some steps in order to strike the right path.
So far as the needs of industry are concerned, I think we have been careful in that regard. My right hon. leader said prior to the last general election-and these words have been referred to frequently in this debate-that no legitimate industry would suffer as a result of the changes which would be made by his administration should he be returned to power. Well, I claim that no industry has suffered, nor will any suffer, as a result of the changes that are made in the .tariff. Is there any suffering evident anywhere? We do not believe it. We believe that it is in the interests of Canadian industry to open foreign markets, to have greater freedom of exchange with other countries. We cannot sell without buying. I see my hon. friend from York (Sir Henry Drayton) laughing, but he knows that what I say is right; we cannot sell without buying. The export business is not a gift, it is 'a matter of trade, and we must be prepared to buy goods from other countries. What is the hon. gentleman muttering about?
The minister is asking me a question it seems, and I suppose he wants an answer.

With our present unforeseen balance against us we have a large amount of outside credits against which we can sell. We have imported many hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of coupons against the interest on which goods can be sold. If my hon. friend does not know that he ought to.
