speechtext:
My hon. friend has
waited until the end of the debate to tell us that we have a balance against us. Let me tell him that he is wrong; we have a balance in our favour.
My hon. friend is putting words inito my mouth and I object to that. I am talking about interest coupons we have to import, and he is thinking only of a visible trade balance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is not the question. I happen to have the floor at the moment and I should like to be allowed to proceed. I say that industry has not suffered, and I go further and say that no industry will suffer, as a result of the tariff changes. A
statement of the Massey-Harris Company issued recently seems to have disappointed hon. gentlemen opposite; they do not like it. They would have liked to see that company close its doors they would like to see blue ruin and disaster in order to achieve political success.
Mr. Speaker-
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At this late hour I must ask hon. gentlemen to be good enough to let me	proceed.	I repeat, my hon. friends
opposite seem to be in partnership with calamity and desolation. We have heard many stories of the chimerical closing of bogus factories, and other statements which Ananias would envy. Now, my hon. friend from Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobin) handed me a few moments ago a letter which is very interesting. On April 1 he wrote to Mr. J. 0. Darche, who last year was president of the board of trade of Sherbrooke, Quebec, and who, I may say, is not a political friend of the government.
Mr. Tobin's letter is as follows:
My dear Darche.-
I see in last Friday and Saturday's papers the statement that there are six manufactures closed down in Sherbrooke on account of the tariff. This was a surprise to me as I never heard any talk about such a state of affairs. I would be very pleased if you could let me. know, if such is the case, the names of those manufactures, etc. In so doing you would oblige.
Yours very truly,
E. Tobin.
Let me read the reply:
Dear Mr. Tobin :
Replying to your letter of the 1st instant re statement made at a meeting of the Rotary Club and Canadian Manufacturers' Association at the Sherbrooke House on the 25th of March last, by Mr. Geo. D. MacKinnon, I beg to report the following. The manufacturers referred to are The Regal Tire Co., The Geo. St. Pierre Co., The Hamilton Shoe Co., The Jenckes Manufacturing Co., The Goupil Chocolate Manufacturing Co., and the Manganese Steel Co.
Now, The Regal Tire Co., The St. Pierre Co., The Hamilton Shoe Co., the Goupil Co., failed from two to five years ago, The Manganese Steel became in financial difficulty lately apparently for other cause than the tariff question, and the Jenckes Co. were absorbed by the Canadian Ingersoll Co. immediately after the war.
It is the opinion of our industrial commissioner that this statement of Mr. Geo. D. MacKinnon of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association was an argument to favour their particular cause.
Hoping this explanation will be of some help to you, I have the honour to be,
Your friend,
J. Omer Darche.
Already the nightmares created by that flood of misrepresentations are vanishing. The idea that people could be carried away

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
by such a panic-mongering campaign was an insane miscalculation, and history will repeat itself in that regard. When in 1897 the Liberal tariff was introduced in this House Sir Charles Tupper, the then leader of the opposition and of the Conservative party, gave expression to the following language:
The result is that this tariff goes into operation and the hon. gentleman knows that the industries of this country are already paralyzed in consequence, while hon. members gloat over the destruction of Canadian industries. I was reading the wail, the sorrowful wail, of these industries in the Montreal Gazette, where one manufacturer after another declared that those industries were ruined, that their mills must close, and that they saw staring them in the face a return to the deplorable state of things that existed when the hon. gentleman who last addressed the House was in charge of the fiscal policy of this country. I say that a deeper wrong was never inflicted upon Canada.
I feel that so far from rejoicing at it from a party standpoint, I deplore from the bottom of my heart the ruin that is going to be inflicted upon the best interests of Canada, and upon its great industries. Still I unhesitatingly say that, from a party point of view, the hon. gentlemen are doing our work; they are showing the people of this country that no reliance can be placed upon the most solemn declarations that they make either in the House or out of it; they are showing the people of this country that, having obtained power, which was all they wished for, they are now prepared to abuse that power at a cost of sacrifice of the industries of Canada.
The very words which we have heard in this House for the last four weeks! And even the good old Montreal Gazette. still doing its work as it was doing it at that time -defending Toryism every morning and telling its tale of woe. Well, such was not the case. Those predictions did not prove true. Indeed they proved so untrue that a few years afterwards those gentlemen were carrying on their campaign by saying: Let well enough alone, we are doing too well to change.
We believe in the tariff changes that we have proposed, and we are. prepared to fight for them. We are going to fight in this House and out of it for the principles embodied in those changes. I am sorry indeed that some of our friends may not agree with us, because, if so, they are going to deprive themselves of the pleasure of carrying on a triumphant fight against the combined forces of Toryism and selfishness and against some watered stock mandarins who masquerade as the champions of Canadian industry.
The propaganda has started; we have it now. I have here the Journal of Commerce of April 3, containing a report of a meeting of the Eastern Manufacturers in Montreal, under the title: "Eastern Manufacturers combining for Tariff Fight: Plan to unite all sections of business and members of political

parties to fight for higher tariff." I quote, these two paragraphs from the report:
The plan when put in operation will probably be modelled on the-
There is a blur at this point-
-of 1911, which so successfully fought reciprocity at that time; and it will include as the principal plank of its platform the commonsense suggestion that all those who think alike on national questions get together for national interests, irrespective of the party labels of individual manufacturers. In this way it is hoped to bring together for the purpose of securing a higher tariff, the business section of the Liberals of Quebec and Conservatives of Ontario whose tariff aims are considered to be identical. The plan would be broad enough to include all classes of business life, on the theory that the interests of classes not directly related to manufacturing interests are in reality bound # up with them. The first-
And I call the attention of hon. members to these words:
The first definite expression of the campaign was a get-together non-political rally held last week in Montreal when four hundred Conservative manufacturers' association delegates from all over Quebec made an impressive demonstration in support of criticism of the present tariff.
Well, this propaganda will not be successful. We will appeal, and I believe successfully, to the manufacturers who have achieved success through hard work and keen business methods, who trusted the Liberal party when it was attacked in the past, who trusted Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he was assailed in the same way as my leader is being assailed today, and who do not believe that it is in the interests of Canadian industry that their association or group should be made an adjunct, or, to use words familiar in this House, a "dilapidated annex" of the Tory party. They realize that there is danger in such an attitude. They know that this country is so vast and has such various and diversified interests that no public man, indeed no progressive business man, should centre his views upon purely local or provincial enterprise and ignore those questions which are fundamental and which must be studied and so dealt with as to make this country prosperous. Those chiefs of industry I think we can successfully appeal to from this higher plane, and I believe that our appeal will be responded to. Our governmental institutions and politics must not be bent in the direction of any class interests, but must be based on the principle of equal justice to all as the only means of safeguarding national peace and norma/ evolution.
I believe that the changes in the tariff will reduce the cost of living substantially and alleviate the troubles of our consumers during the crisis which they are passing through as

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
the result of conditions which are prevailing throughout the world. Pending a gradual recuperation of the purchasing power of the nation, the obvious remedy, and the only remedy, is a reduction in prices. Ask any influential man in our rural districts and he will tell you that the farmer is suffering from the high price of everything he has to buy. That is the reason that so many cannot make both ends meet and are attracted by the lure of foreign countries. Any policy which will decrease the cost of living and the prices of 2 a.m. what the farmer has to buy will afford him most necessary relief. Hon. gentlemen opposite have referred many times to the exodus from Canada, to the fact that so many of our fellow-countrymen are going to the United States. Surely they do not expect the people to believe that those who left us two or three years, or even one year, ago did so on account of the present tariff changes? The primary cause of this exodus is the high price of everything and the lack of purchasing power, which I hope will be partially remedied by the decrease of taxation and the resulting reduction in prices. Industry and agriculture must not quarrel with each other; they must help each other in the interests of production. The Canadian nation has its roots in the soil. I was reading a few days ago in the English Review the words of Lord Milner, who in a preface to a pamphlet on the place of agriculture in the life of a nation wrote:
Unless we are prepared to make a serious and sustained effort to preserve it, agriculture in Great Britain seems doomed to progressive decadence, but if we acquiesce in the decay of agriculture that is to incur national disaster.
Those words are much ti-uer when applied to our Canadian agriculture. I may remind hon. gentlemen that there is a difference between agriculture and the other industries in this, if another industry than agriculture declines or disappears it may be replaced by another industry, but there is no substitute for agriculture.
It has been suggested that the reductions made-in the tariff this year have been made to answer the demands of the western farmers, and even to cajole them. Mr. Speaker, were it true that these reductions are made solely to give satisfaction to a large section of the Canadian community and in order to achieve a greater unity in this country, they would have much value, but the western farmer is not alone in his claim for a lower tariff on the instruments of production. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) will not be surprised if I remind him
that he made a tour of this country in 1920 as an investigator for the purpose of getting all the information necessary for a revision of the tariff. Indeed in the session following, we were told in the Speech from the Throne that there would be a revision of the tariff. During my hon. friend's peregrinations he came to the good old city of Quebec, where he listened to much testimony that was given before him, especially by the manufacturers; but the farmers came too. and I have here a copy of the evidence that was taken before my hon. friend. The leaders of the agricultural societies of the province of Quebec appeared before the commission, and I see attached to a memorandum they presented the names of:
N. Garneau, President Breeders' Association of the Province of Quebec and Member of the Council of Agriculture.
Aug. Trudel, Manager Co-operative Central de Agriculture de Quebec.
Frank Byrne, President of the Breeders' Association of the Quebec District.
Louis Lavallee, Gerant de la societe Cooperative Agricole des producteur de semence de Quebec.
John Hay, M.P.P. Argenteuil and Member of the Council of Agriculture of Quebec.
Georges Bouchard, Professor at the Agricultural College of Sainte Anne de la Pocatiere, P.Q.
C. A. Fournier, M.P., Bellechasse.
Elizee Theriault, M.P.P. for L'lslet Gustave Boyer, M.P., President Dariy-Men's Association of the Province of Quebec and President Maple Sugar Co-operative Society of the province of Quebec.
I see that Mr. Garneau appeared before the commission and said:
The intensified difficulty of the farmers' position resulting from the 'high prices of machinery and of the different materials and merchandise necessary to agricultural operations and to the requirements of the family justify the demand for a general lowering of the tariff on all the articles required for the cultivation of the soil and for the support of the family.
Then they give a list of the instruments of production which they want to make free or on which they wish a reduction of duties. Mr. Garneau also says:
The reciprocity claimed by the farmers in 1911 was combatted by the manufacturers, which did not, however prevent the great majority of the electors of Quebec from favouring the measure. In 1917 one of the principal articles of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's programme included the lowering of the duty on all agricultural implements and the promise of a tariff reform which while sufficiently protecting the Canadian manufacturing industries would have greatly improved the condition of the farmer, of the workman, and of the Canadian consumer in general.
I could read what other gentlemen said before the commission, but it is practically the same thing. So the demand for a lowering of duties, on agricultural implements and the instruments of production generally does not come exclusively from the west as my hon. friends opposite like to repeat under so many
The Budget-Mr. Lapointe

different circumstances. Now if a farmer saves 825.00 on the purchase of his implements, he will be able to buy goods which he could not afford to buy otherwise. This means increased production for other manufacturers. These are the considerations which have influenced the government in proposing the changes which they have submitted to the House. The responsibility of many of our critics is to their board of directors and to their shareholders. We are responsible to the people of Canada. Our responsibility is even to the future of Canada, to those future Canadians to whom we want to bequeath a united country.
My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) whom I am pleased to see in his seat at this late hour, told us the other day of what he called a romance, and indeed it was a fine piece of fiction. There is another fiction which I would like to say a few words upon, although my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has already alluded to it.
I was elected to this parliament in 1904. I was a young man coming here, with all the enthusiasm of my age. I was proud then as I am to-day to call myself a Liberal. By temperament, by training,; by aptitude, I could not be anything else.
But, sir, I do not hesitate to say that my greatest incentive, my real source of inspiration was the unbounded admiration I had for the then illustrious leader of the Liberal party, my late chief, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I have followed him to the very last moment of his life. My political principles, the things I hold dear in public life, I have learned and received from him and even now his revered memory is a fiery cross which lights the way through the difficulties we have to face. I say it is a crime on the part of those who were strangers to his spirit and opposed to his policy, who fought against him, sometimes in a most unfair way to endeavour to use his name to cover their mistaken policies and propound very illiberal doctrines. He devoted forty-five yeans of his life to the pursuit of freedom and the advance of right and we who were his associates, his companions, his devoted followers, his disciples, will not allow those former opponents of his to misuse his noble figure in support of their reactionary principles. I could quote the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, prior to 1896 and since that time. They would be worth publishing and will be published some day, but I do not think it is necessary that I should read them here - to-night. I do intend, however, to read the words which my right hon. leader read because they were

uttered in the last speech Sir Wilfrid Laurier delivered. I may perhaps ask the liberty to read those words again in order that they may be included in my remarks. Addressing the Eastern Liberal Ontario Association on January 14, 1919, Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke as follows:
In this country, Sir, Liberals have always been the disciples of the British people on the question of commercial freedom. Indeed, many years ago-when you recall that time to-day in the resolution which was passed upon this subject at the convention of 1893, we declared against the principle of protection, and when we had the opportunity we lived up to our declaration. Sir, it has always been made a cause of reproach to us that when in office we did not adopt but were recreant to our declaration. Such a reproach cannot reach us. We were not recreant, We proceeded step by step towards the goal, always keeping it in view, never imposing a duty for protection's sake only but always acting on the principle or the basis of a tariff for revenue and revenue only. This was our policy in the p$st, it is our policy to-day, and we have taken this occasion to re-affirm it.
And we, to-day although we have not the fame of our lustrous leader declare to-day that this is our policy and that it will prevail.
Now, Sir Wilfrid Laurier had to fight many elections in the course of his public life, and he had to fight many after 1896. If you take the trouble, as I did, to go to the library and read the electioneering pamphlets issued by the Conservative party in all the elections which followed 1896, you will see what hon. gentlemen opposite thought of the tariff policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I will not read the extracts I have here on account of the lateness of the hour, but I promise to the electors of my province and of the rest of Canada that they will be published. Will you permit me to read simply a little song which was published in the Conservative campaign pamphlet of 1911; it is very interesting:
Cheer boys cheer for R. L. Borden,
He's our leader staunch and true,
For he's bound to win the day
Over Sir Wilfrid Laurier
And the members of the annexation crew.
I will not recall what was done when the British preference, what was done when reciprocity was proposed by the Canadian government led by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and by the present Minister of Finance. May I refer though to a little incident. In 1902 my right hon. leader of that time was absent attending a conference, I think it was the Imperial conference in London, and a member of his cabinet-a very able man in every way but who had on tariff matters the same views as the present right hon. leader of the opposition -during Sir Wilfrid Laurier's absence had

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
preached the principles of high protection in the province of Quebec, and I think in the rest of the country. The first thing that was done by Sir Wilfrid Laurier on his return was to ask for the resignation of that member of his cabinet. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite claim that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was asserting their views in tariff matters. Let me tell them in all earnestness: Hands off the sacred name of Laurier. Leave his untarnished and glorious memory alone.
There are a couple of things I should like to refer to. The hour is late but it will be my only opportunity to do it. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), I am afraid he is not here to-night-

Before my hon.
friend leaves that subject would he mind placing on record the statement made by the minister, who he says was read out of his party, regarding an understanding the Liberal party had with the manufacturers prior to the election of 1896. Make the story complete while you are at it.

I do not know anything about it. My hon. friend seems to have a fountain of knowledge regarding matters that I am not familiar with at all. This is the first I ever heard of such a thing and I cannot give him the information asked for. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has a fondness for attacking the French treaty. He did it last * year and the House will remember that he spoke about bronze powder at the time. He came back this year and gave statistics which I am afraid I must describe as most unfair. Then he gave the amounts which would have been collected if that treaty had not been agreed to, and he said that there was a considerable amount which had been lost by the country. Well, Mr. Speaker, I discovered a peculiar thing. Instead of comparing 'the duties wjhieh are collected under the present treaty with those collected under the treaty when my hon. friends were in power, he made the comparison with the general tariff which is most unfair, so unfair that my hon. friend referring to silk fabrics from France said the amount collected was $279,093 where as he said, the amount that would have been collected should be $330,004. Well, Mr. Speaker, the amount that would have been collected for imports when the former government were in power, under the old modus vivendi, would have been $259,-
289.52. That is to say that we have collected under the present treaty on silk fabrics $24,000 more than would have been collected under the old treaty. Well, sir, the amount which would have been collected under the treaty in force when the late government was in power, and which was replaced by the present treaty, is $490,548.85. On champagne the hon. member said we lost a revenue of $32,222.20, when as a matter of fact there is a loss of revenue of only $7,476.74, being a difference of $24,745.46 between the figures wrongly given by my hon. friend.

There is another subject on which my statements have been challenged, and to which I wish to refer. The right hon. leader of the opposition toured the country last summer and fall, and said in all his speeches, referring to a statement of mine, that the debt of Canada per capita was less than the debt of all the other dominions and even Great Britain; and he said it was true, but he stated that Mr. Lapointe did not state the reason why our taxation was higher than that of these countries. I have taken the first opportunity to deny that our taxation was higher than that of Great Britain and the other dominions, and that statement has been challenged not only by my right hon. friend the

leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), but by the press which is devoted to him in the country. I remember that the Ottawa Journal used rather strong language regarding me in that respect. They thought that I was deliberately misrepresenting the facts, or displaying gross ignorance. I have taken the trouble to inquire about it, and I state tonight that our taxation per capita is less than that of Great Britain and the other British dominions, and that taxation per head in the United Kingdom is $101.59, being $79.37 for central government and $22.22 for local government.

Does that include the provincial government?

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no provincial
government in the United Kingdom. I am quoting England at present. In the Commonwealth of Australia the taxation per head is $67.06, the revenue of the Commonwealth being S43.09 per head, and the state revenue being 815.78 per head, the municipal revenue $8.19 per head. New Zealand has a taxation of $76.75 per capita, the Dominion revenue from taxation being $60.33, and the local governing body $16.02. In reference to our local taxation in Canada, unfortunately we cannot have exact figures as to rural municipal taxation as correctly as they have in the other countries. The tax of the Dominion per capita is $36.67; of the provinces, $6,85; of the urban municipalities, $12.65. or a total of $56.17. The Bureau of Statistics adds this note:
The rural municipalities are unquestionably much more lightly taxed than the urban. However, their expenditures for education are fairly heavy. Doubtless in the aggregate they raise as much in taxation as do the provincial governments. All that can be said is that the total taxation of Canada is between $60 and $65 per head of population-probably $63 would be a fairly good estimate.
So our taxation per capita is lower than that of the British Empire, not only the United Kingdom, but the other dominions as well.
But there is more. The hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) asked me what was the taxation in the United States, and I did not know at the time. He told me that I should make the comparison with the United States. I have in my hand the Bankers Magazine of April, 1924, and this is what I find as regards the details of taxation in the United States. The article which is entitled "Your Government" by Carlton P. Fuller:
The final summing up shows annual taxes of $68 per person, $29 going to the federal government, and $39 to the state and local governments. Putting it another way, $7,000,000,000 out of a total national income of $63,000,000,000 go for taxes.
What are the municipal taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All is included in that. So that in Canada our taxation as estimated at $63 per capita is even lighter than the taxation in the United States. I hope the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) will go into all those places where he spoke last summer and make the real statement about the taxation of Canada. If you, Mr. Speaker, were to take a leaf out of his book and distribute medals at the end of the session to those of us who are specially virtuous, he would not qualify as regards accuracy in making public statements. As to the Ottawa Journal, of course I am a humble public man
and I cannot have the license of the press in expressing myself. All I can say is that they have shown a peculiar lack of accurate information in this respect. No, Canada is not what the "whispers of death" and the "scaremongers" are describing it to be. I have before me the latest figures of trade which have been given to me by the Department of Trade and Commerce. We have total exports amounting to $1,058,553,297, being a considerable balance of trade in our favour.
Employment in this country is not what it has been described to be by my hon. friend opposite. I am sorry the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) is not in his seat. I would give him some information about conditions in Hamilton that he does not seem to know. In his speech he read a statement showing the reductions that have taken place in the staffs of a number of Hamilton industries in the period from 1920 to 1923. He said:
Not only does this statement illustrate the unfortunate results that have already occurred, but it serves to show other changes along this line which may be expected in future if reductions of the tariff are continued.
He placed on Hansard a list of some twenty-seven plants, branches of American industries located and manufacturing in Hamilton, and he gave a tabulated statement showing the number of employees in the various plants in the year 1919 and the number of employees in the same plants in the year 1923. I do not think this was absolutely fair, because in 1919 all the manufacturers were operating to a reasonable extent, manufacturing articles for the rest of the world. Our government was then lending money to European countries, and that money was going to them in the shape of articles manufactured by Canadian manufacturers. But my hon. friend should give the figures as they are now. Steps were taken, I think in the Labour Department, to secure a check on the number of employees in those plants to-day, and the figures secured within the last week indicate the condition of employment in that city. The hon. member stated that the Hamilton branch of the American-Canadian Company, New York, had 175 employees in 1923. It is found that in May, 1924, the company employs 188. He stated that the Hamilton branch of the Canadian Horseshoe Company in 1923 had 80 employees. It is found that at present the company employs 102. He stated that the Hamilton branch of the Chipman-Holton Knitting Company employed 400 employees last year. It is found that at present this company employs 450. He stated that the
The Budget-Mr. Lapointe

Hamilton branch of the Frost Steel and Wire Company, Cleveland, in 1923 had 100 employees, and it is found that at present this company employs 200. He stated that the Hamilton branch of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company in 1923 had 250 employees. It is found at present that the company employs 296. He stated that the Hamilton branch of the Imperial Cotton Company in 1923 had 200 employees, and it is found at present that it employs 290. He stated that the Hamilton branch of the Standard Underground Cable Company had 100 employees last year. It is found at present that it employs 180.
The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), speaking of the International Harvester Company, said:
It will now close up its factory in Hamilton, manufacture in Chicago and just ship its agricultural implements over into Canada. The money invested in the Hamilton plant can be considered wasted and the plant can now be scrapped.
The hon. member for West Hamilton stated that the branches of the International Harvester Company of Chicago and the International Plow Works of Chicago employed 450 men in 1923. He will no doubt be very much interested and elated to know that the investigation of the past week shows that instead of . the 450 employees who were employed last year, there are at present 1160 employees in the plant of the company at Hamilton, or an increase of 710 employees over last year.
As regards our trade with Great Britain, owing to a propaganda that is carried on in my province at the present time, I find it necessary to put these figures on Hansard. Our imports from the United Kingdom for the year ended March 31 last were $153,581,716. while our imports were $360,094,021, being a balance of trade in our favour of more than double. Some people are talking of British goods that are dumped into this country. The figures show that we are selling to Britain more than twice what we are buying from her. Some people .have a queer idea of what the British preference is; they think it is something that has been instituted in the interests of Great Britain. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it was instituted in the interests of Canada for the purpose of developing trade with Britain. That trade has been developed and we are gainers by it, because we are selling to Britain more than twice what we are buying from her. So that it is preposterous to say that because we have no particular preference in Britain we should not shape our own policy in the way we have shaped it. Our goods are admitted free in the markets of Britain and her goods pay a duty coming into Canada.

Britain has no tariff against us whereas the United States maintain a high tariff to the exclusion of our exports. I contend therefore that it is right that a preference should be given to that country into which our goods can be shipped without paying a duty, in order that we may build up a trade with her. The argument in regard to depreciated currency countries is not in my opinion a good one. I have never been able to appreciate the contention that a country whose currency is depreciated benefits by reason of the fact, as though it could enrich a nation to become bankrupt. We have been buying from these depreciated currency countries. We are told that our market is flooded with goods coming from Germany, Belgium and other countries whose currencies are depreciated. What are the figures? What is the result of our exchange trade with those countries? Belgium bought from us last year $17,452,442 worth of goods and sold to us $5,340,875 worth; a balance of trade in our favour of three times more in exports than imports. From France we imported goods to the value of $15,770,145 and exported to that country $18,879,097. That left a balance of trade in our favour of $3,000,000. I come now to Germany, and the argument in regard to that country is one we hear everywhere: we are told that German goods flood our markets. Well, we sold to Germany last year $16,153,673 worth of goods and imported $5,379,737. Italy imported from us $18,501,578, and we purchased from Italy only $1,849,844. So that there was a balance of trade in our favour in exports eighteen times greater than our imports. I say, Sir, that we are not losing by not blocking the avenues of trade with those countries. We are selling to them a good deal more than we are buying from them, and they have to pay high prices by reason of their depreciated currency. In other words, it is they and not we who are suffering; and I implore Canadian business men not to try to block the avenues of trade with any country. In this regard I want- to quote the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in a speech delivered by him at the Windsor Hotel, Montreal, on May 29, 1912:
Oh! ye of little faith! Oh! ye Canadian business men, who refused to open wide the avenues of trade, I have more faith in you than you have in yourselves. Will you tell me that Canadians are not the equals of Americans? Will you tell me that in a fair field we cannot compete with them and hold our own against them? Until you tell me that Canadians are not the equals of Americans, I refuse to believe that we made a mistake last year.
I hasten to conclude these rather lengthy remarks. Canada is a young country and a young country cannot be immobilized: its very life consists in motion and progress. The

The Budget-Mr. Caldwell
function of Liberalism is to recognize this state of mind, to bind it with prudence and safety-in making reform and avoiding danger. Our most powerful agent of reconstruction and recovery is peace among Canadians, and you cannot have peace economically or otherwise unless you extend social justice to all. Canada is a smiling country. Let it be a nation of nine million smiles, and I am willing to include my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition in that glorious demonstration of national cheerfulness.

speechtext:
If I felt that an apology was necessary on my part for contributing to the debate at this late hour it would be the fact that I have occupied, not only during this session but in the last session as well, as little time as any hon. member has done. I have been particularly impressed with the speeches that have been delivered in this ddbate, although the whole discussion has been somewhat like one of the serial stories that one reads in the magazines; it is difficult to keep in mind just what transpired in the first chapter. However, I do not wish to review the whole story, but I shall content myself with dealing with a few things that have been said in the debate. I do not propose spending very much time in any discussion of the budget, which has been very well considered by hon. gentlemen in this group, the attitude of the Progressive party having been clearly defined not only by its leader (Mr. Forke) but also by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and other hon. gentlemen on this side who have spoken. I was very much impressed with some of the sentences that fell from the lips of the Prime Minister this afternoon as well as from the hon. member for Marquette, both having largely stated the same views in certain respects. I refer particularly to the plea for unity in this country, if we expect to attain to that full stature of nationhood which is ours by right, by the gifts of Nature, and by Providence. I heartily agree with the Prime Minister's statement that the aim of the government should be to unify or harmonize the different elements in this country. With that feeling I desire to associate myself, although there are some very prominent men in Canada who seem to devote their whole energy to making this ideal an impossibility by trying to set one interest and one section of the country against the other. In this respect I wish to quote from a speech made in the House last year, which by the way I had not the pleasure of hearing. As a matter of fact, I was unaware of it having been made until after prorogation when I discovered that 139
it had been printed in pamphlet form and distributed where the hon. member who delivered it evidently thought it would do the most good, or, from my point of view, the most harm. Now I quote from a speech made in this House on February 8 last year by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter). I will not quote the whole speech because a great deal of it is not worth repeating.
Which member for St. John?

The member who spoke to-night. I could define him so you would know beyond question if I thought it necessary. That part of his speech which I am now about to quote relates to the restoration of the Crowsnest pass agreement and its effect on the eastern farmer. This quotation will be found on page 137 of last year's Hansard:
In the parliamentary agreement of last year potatoes were not mentioned. Now, can you tell me anything that distinguishes the pian who grows grain from the man who grows potatoes? Is there any reason why a burden should be even partially lifted from the one and yet allowed to remain upon the other? I know my hon. friends will not say there is any reason. Well, then, what happened? The government's action paralyzed the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the potato growers of New Brunswick could not seek relief in that quarter. Railway rates were so much reduced that the railway companies, which have to pay their bills like every other company, had to get money from some source and the only source of course, of their revenue is the passengers and freight they handle. Therefore the Railway Commission could afford no relief by lowering the freight rates on potatoes or lumber, except upon one commodity only coming under the classification of building materials, namely, bricks, and in this instance the reduction was very small.
It is just possible that the hon. member was ignorant of the actual conditions when he made that statement; I hope so. Two months after the Crowsnest pass agreement was restored by legislation, and about five months before the hon. member made this speech, the potato growers of New Brunswick-whom he refers to almost with tears in his eyes-got a greater reduction in freight rates than the farmers of the West secured on their grain. We obtained a reduction of over 25 per cent on our export rate, and all the potatoes we moved that year were for export. I shall refer to the Crowsnest pass agreement a little later because even tonight the hon. member stated:
The government makes the Crowsnest pass sacrifice for the benefit of the West.
It has been said that that agreement was only of benefit to the western grain grower. I therefore propose to show the benefit this agreement was to the eastern manufacturer

The Budget-Mr. Caldwell

and fruit grower in comparison with its benefit to the wheat grower. As we all know, the reduction of the rate on wheat was 3 cents per hundred pounds regardless of the length of haul, and in a great many cases the haul was long. We got a reduction of 6 cents per hundred pounds on a short haul on a rate that was only 23-J cents a hundred pounds originally.. This made our reduction over 25 per cent of the original rate. To show the absurdity of the statement made by the hon. member-and I hope he was ignorant of the facts when he made it, because I would hate to think that any hon. member would make such a statement otherwise-to show the absurdity of the statement I have worked out the reductions per acre. I have taken twenty bushels of wheat per acre as the average yield, but I think it is above the average. That would be equivalent to twelve hundred pounds, or a reduction of 36 cents per acre to the 'western grain grower. Taking the average yield of potatoes at 100 barrels to the acre-which would be small, the yield last year running in some cases as high as 150 barrels to the acre,-this would mean 16,500 pounds, or a reduction of $9.90 per acre. In other words, a gain to the potato farmer of $9.90 per acre, as against a gain to the wheat grower of 36 cents per acre.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that two years ago I moved a resolution in this House asking the government to establish frostproof facilities at St. John in order that we might get our potatoes to market during the winter season at a rate that would return the farmer something for his product. I had some difficulty in convincing the government of the necessity for establishing these facilities. I made several trips to Ottawa as well as to St. John, and at last almost despairing . of being able to convince the government single-handed, I asked the Secretary of the Board of Trade of the city of St. John to call a meeting of his board, which he kindly did. It was well attended, but the hon. member for St, John, although he professes to have the interests of the potato-growers of New Brunswick so much at heart, did not put in an appearance. The members of the Board of Trade realizing that these facilities at St. John would very much increase the traffic through the port'-a traffic which was at that time going through the port of Boston owing to our lack of facilities-got behind the project. As I say, the hon. member for St. John did not attend, although this meeting was for the purpose of urging the government
IMr. CsldweU.J
to furnish facilities in his own port and to bring traffic to it, a subject upon which he is so insistent, and in which I heartily concur with him. I have estimated that the benefit to the potato-growers of New Brunswick would amount to 75 cent per barrel. As confirmation of this estimate, I shall quote an extract from a letter from one of our shippers who was very anxious to have these facilities established, giving his view of what it would mean to the potato-growers of New Brunswick. By the way, this saving of 75 cents a barrel would mean a saving of $75 an acre, because we would get the short rail haul to St. John. When we shipped through Boston we not only had the long rail haul, but we had to pay the freight in American funds from point of shipment clear to Cuba, which in 1921 meant a discount of 15 per cent on our money. The discount is less now. This shipper has been shipping to Cuba for twelve or fourteen years, from Boston in cold weather and from St. John when there was no danger of frost. In writing me to urge upon the government to establish those frost-proof facilities he said:
Now, all we need is the government to do what they should do for this province, furnish us frost-proof facilities at the port of St. John and a line of tween deck steamers out of St. John. They will not only be helping out the revenue of the Canadian Merchant Marine, but such a boom to the farmers and shippers.
This is the interesting part:
If we had a rate of $1 per barrel from St. John to Havana we could be paying the farmer in New Brunswick to-day $2 for potatoes instead of 75 cents. Not only this but we would have a market which is a regular market for our products.
He estimated that the saving at that time would' be $1.25 per barrel. As I pointed out the discount on our money then was greater than it is to-day. However, I think, Mr. Speaker, you will admit that I am making a very conservative estimate in placing the saving to the shipper at 75 cents per barrel by the establishment of frost-proof facilities at St. John. Therefore I say that any hon. member who will stand up in this House and make a statement of that kind, if he knew the facts, is certainly not trying to promote national harmony.
With regard to the restoration of the Crows-nest pass agreement, the statement has been made repeatedly that it is a 3 a.m. benefit only to the western grain-growers. I shall quote from the agreement itself and then give some figures as to the freight saving to other people besides the western grain grower. This is the agreement:

which I would ask permission of the House to place on Hansard. Take Montreal and Toronto to Winnipeg, the shortest haul possible for agricultural implements to get the 'benefit of the Crowsnest rate. Very little of the implements would stay at Fort William. I want to quote the rate to Edmonton from the Ontario group. The rate was 164^ cents per 100 pounds, as compared with 148 cents, or a reduction of 16-J cents per 100 pounds, as compared with 3 cents per 100 pounds on wheat. From the Montreal group to Edmonton prior to the Crowsnest pass agreement the rate was 170 cents. After the Crowsnest pass agreement that was reduced on January 1, 1898, to 153j, or a reduction of 17 per hundred, another reduction which the railways are not compelled to make under the agreement. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member in his speech said that the action of the government in restoring the Crowsnest pass agreement was to paralyze the railway commission, and therefore the potato growers were not able to get any relief. We did not, as a matter of fact, even have to apply to the commission. Two of the shippers from New Brunswick and myself went to Montreal and interviewed the Traffic Department of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways and got this reduction without applying to the railway commission and we got it in one afternoon, so if the railway commission was paralyzed, the railways were not.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need to labour that point any further. I think I have proved to any reasonable man that this agreement is not all in favour of the western grain grower. But when the Crowsnest pass agreement goes into effect on the 6th July next, if it does become effective-and I see no reason why it should not -our manufacturing friends from eastern Canada and the fruit growers will certainly be able to get into the western market. There is no question about that. I am sorry I have not the rates on apples from the Maritime provinces to Montreal. I have taken the rates on potatoes from the Maritime provinces to Montreal, and I think the rates are practically the same. The rate from the furthest point in New Brunswick from where potatoes were shipped to Montreal, in 1917, was 19 cents per hundred pounds, and in 1920 it was 38i cents per hundred pounds, and the Crowsnest pass rate provides that from any point in eastern Canada the reduction shall be 33J per cent from the regular rate, which would mean two-thirds of 19 cents in 1917, which would be 12f cents added to the 59 cents from Montreal to Winnipeg, which would mean that you could ship apples to Winnipeg from any point in the Maritime provinces to Winnipeg for 71f cents per hundred pounds, while the rate from the Okanagan valley to Winnipeg is $1.13. In view of those facts, I do not think that any man can contend that the Crowsnest pass agreement is a discrimination even against the eastern farmer who is growing fruit. We do not ship potatoes to the West because they grow their own potatoes, but they cannot grow apples. Here is an opening for the fruit grower.
I had another table giving "the comparative rates from Montreal west and from Vancouver east. If I am allowed to place this on Hansard I will not take time to read it.
Hear, hear.

I have one or two other matters I wish to refer to. We have heard very doleful wails indeed from our friends to my right with regard to the plight of the Canadian manufacturer and what this tariff will do to him. I am not contending that the tariff is the sole cause of the conditions that I am going to place on the records of this House just now. I hold in my hand a copy of the Royal Gazette of the date of April 30 and I find 22 farms advertised for sale under mortgage in New Brunsrvick. I wonder if people who are wailing about the manufacturers have any thought for the agriculturists of this country. I do not think if a man wished that he could attribute this to the present

The Budget-Mr. Caldwell
budget-because a man does not get sold out under a mortgage in one year, possibly not in ten years. A man who loans money on mortgage wants to make an investment, and as long as the farmer is able to pay his interest he is not sold out. I have never known of a case where foreclosure was made if the farmer was able to pay the interest. But here are 22 farms advertised for sale in one issue of the Royal Gazette for April.
What size farms?

It is covering pretty well the province. These are not all the farms advertised for sale in the province. I have a copy of the Weekly Mail, Fredericton, New Brunswick, in which there were four farms advertised for sale under mortgage, in the one issue. If you pick up any weekly paper in that province you will find these advertisements. People will say that that is a pretty doleful picture, and I am glad the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is in his place, because I want to quote from the Monthly Bulletin of Agricultural Statistics, February 15, 1924, from the crop reports of the province summarized from the reports of the crop correspondents, January 31, 1924, as follows:
Maritime provinces.-Throughout the Maritime provinces, the open winter has been very beneficial for live stock. There is an abundance of feed everywhere and cattle are in good condition. The market has been dull, and farmers selling are realizing but low prices. A correspondent at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, writes: "In many cases farmers deem it more economical to slaughter some of their stock rather than winter it with no prospect of market next spring". Prices for lambs and sheep are about the same as last year, whilst those of swine dropped badly during the summer. Poultry prices were particularly disappointing at Christmas time on account of the mild unseasonable weather during December. Buildings have increased in value the last few years, while farm land has decreased. Help is hired by the day, as farmers cannot afford to pay wages since the drop in value of farm products. Some farmers talk of leaving their land if conditions do not improve.
I am pleased to see some members from Nova Scotia in their seats. I attended with them a meeting in this House not long ago to listen to a discourse by a man who had been making a survey of vacant lands in the Maritime provinces, where there was a possibility of settling immigrants. I do not remember the number of farms he mentioned in any one given county, but I know it ran into large figures. He was asked how many of these farms had complete buildings, and I think he answered 60 per cent. I think one of the members from Nova Scotia asked the question, and received the answer that 60 per cent had complete buildings and a large number were vacant, and they were surveying with the idea of settling the newcomers on the farm, so that the statement that many farmers would leave the farms if conditions do not improve is mild indeed. I will not deal with all the provinces, but I will take the province of Quebec, because we have been told it is the most prosperous in the Dominion, and possibly the farmers in Quebec are in the best circumstances of all the farmers in the Dominion. The report from Quebec reads as follows:
Owing to the mild weather of the first part of the season, the supply of fodder was conserved, and the cattle were kept in good condition. The value of farms and of cattle has declined during the last few years. There is practically no sale for cattle and horses. Milch cows and poultry are about the only descriptions yielding any revenue. Correspondents state that if the situation does not improve, many farmers will have to give up their land.
Lambs are the best sellers and the prices quoted for wool show some increase over last year.
This is the interesting part of it:
Very few farm labourers are hired by the year, and farmers, where possible, manage without help, as they cannot afford to pay wages.
I do not know whether our city men realize what this means to a farmer; but I know-and I have farmed under those conditions years ago as well as recently-about not being able to hire farm help. It means that the wife must go out and help on the farm to do work that the man cannot do alone. It means, in all too many cases, that children are kept from school who should be in school and are thereby deprived of getting an education, which feature is the saddest of all.
By the way, I am sorry that the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) is not present, because I have a little crow to pluck with him about farm help in the Maritime provinces in the harvest season. Last year, just about the time when we got ready to harvest our potato crop, which is the crop for which we require the most help, a crop that takes a great deal of help, I saw the usual advertisement of cheap farm excursions to the Canadian West for farm help. I immediately sat down and wrote to the minister calling his attention to this, also calling Ins attention to the fact that, due to depressed times in the Maritime provinces and to the lure of good wages in the United States, many of our young men had left the Maritime provinces and gone to the United States; that help was very scarce. Most of our farmers in the potato growing belt hire their men by the summer; they have to do so because there is a continuous summer's work in cultivating and spraying potatoes. What happens when those posters are put up on fences, barns and every other place where they can stick them,
The Budget-Mr. Caldwell

advertising a cheap rate to the Canadian West? Your hired man puts in his team at six o'clock and he is in such a hurry, he has hardly time to feed them. He tells you that he is going on that harvest excursion next morning. That is after he has been paid good wages all summer and possibly been not overly busy all the time, so that he may be available in the rush season for the potato harvest. I got a reply from the Minister of Railways and Canals stating that this was a matter, not for the government, but for the railway management. I do not agree With the minister. In the matter of inducing people to move from one part of the country to another, it is not for the railway management but for the government to take means to see that help is evenly distributed. If they endeavour to get help for some part of the country that is in need of it, I hope they will not rob the Maritime provinces of the few men whom they are able to retain for the harvest in the fall of the year. If they need help for the western harvest fields -and I realize they do and I do not object to their getting it-let them bring it from where they can get it without robbing the Maritime provinces. Let them go to the bread line in the cities. Of course, I realize that very few of those men will go to the country; they want to be able to go to the pictures at night.
I wish to quote from the records of the special committee on Agricultural Conditions which sat last year to show the other side of the picture. I have endeavoured to give, as briefly as I can, just what is happening to agriculturists in the Maritime provinces, and I think we have had proof enough of conditions in the other provinces. Last year we had all classes of people before us. Some were summoned and some appeared voluntarily. I want to quote from the statements of some manufacturers who were before the committee. I do not wish to be unfair to anybody, nor call particular attention to any manufacturer in Canada and, therefore, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will omit the names. This particular manufacturer who 5'ppeared before our committee painted a very doleful picture of the condition of his industry for the two previous years. We took his statement and we believed it as being possibly correct. He did not, however, state that they had lost money because they could not manufacture the article that they were manufacturing for the prices that they were receiving, but they had lost money because they were not selling; they were doing no business and they were maintaining a big overhead

which was eating up, not only their profits, but their capital. After listening to this very patiently, our chairman asked this question: You brought forward a rather doleful picture of the last two years, and I said, to be fair, we should have a ten-year statement. Do you think there is any objection to giving that?-A. I think I have that, Mr. Chairman, and if you would like to consider it, I will pass it to you, and I would like you to consider it yourself, or with any members of the committee, but I prefer not to have it on the record.
That is, he offered to hand it to the chairman to consider it himself or with any member of his committee, but he refused to have it put on the record. If his condition was bad, why would he refuse to give us the required information. Because no man, I do not care how sharp he is, could form an opinion of the condition of any business by the condition during the two years of which he had given us the operation and cost in very minute detail. We had, however, before us another manufacturer who was more frank, and with your permission, Sir, without giving the name, I will also read a few questions and answers from this man's evidence. The first question and answer which I wish to quote are as follows:
I think you told us your capital at the start was $60,000?-A. $125,000.
Q. $60,000 paid up in cash?
Q. What is your present worth?-A.-
This company was formed in 1903 and had been in operation for eighteen years at the time when this evidence was given.
A. Our present worth on July 31, 1922, surplus $12,500,000, capital, $7,000,000,-about $20,000,000.
That is quite interesting. Starting with a capital of 160,000, they had increased their worth to $20,000,000 in working capital and in the cost of their plant. We were naturally quite anxious to know how this capital had been increased from $60,000 to $20,000,000. There is, however, another question which comes first:
Q. How much dividends have you paid on that?-A. Over what period?
Q. In the whole period?-A. $10,000,000 in cash and $6,000,000 in stock.
The next answer is very interesting:
Q. How has that capital increased to the present amount?-A. By earnings. There was never any fresh money taken in.
I will admit that that is a very frank statement. Starting with a capital of $60,000, admitting there was no further capital taken in, they had increased their worth to $20,000,000. besides paying to the shareholders $10,000,000 in actual cash dividends.

What line of business
was that?

The Budget-Mr. Caldwell

Manufacturer of automobiles, and by the way I think there should be a reduction in automobiles this year. We require cheap automobiles and especially trucks. In New Brunswick, due to the shortage and high cost of help, many of our farmers buy trucks to haul their potatoes to market when they live any distance from the railway, and I think it would be a boon to the farmers to take the duty off trucks and cheap cars. I say that in view of some of these statements it is unfair for hon. gentlemen to accuse the government of any attempt to secure the support of the Progressives in this House through a reduction in the duties on argicultural implements and other tools of industry. I would strongly commend to the careful perusal of my hon. friends the evidence that was given before the special committee on Agriculture last year, and unless their hearts are made of stone I tlnnk they will hardly ever again object to anything that will help the agriculturists out of their present difficult position. I am going to quote a part of a letter which I have received from a gentleman in New Brunswick, and I will not refuse to give his name if it is asked for. This gentleman is not a farmer, and I think he must have been reading the evidence that was given before that special committee last year. He says:
I have been a manufacturer and merchant, doing business in the Maritime provinces for thirty-five years, president and secretary for Connors Bros. Limited for twenty-five years, president and secretary for the Maritime Steamship Co. for fifteen years, president of Sturgeon Cove Lumber Co., Ltd. for ten years, and several other corporate and private companies in the Maritime provinces, would say:-
I have been a believer in a high protective tariff in the past for manufacturers, such as the United States for home practice. But times have changed, and we must study our best interest and lay party lines aside, because our people that have been educated in all lines of business are leaving Canada and going to United States. High tariff is all right for them, but bad for Canada, because we cannot sell our fish, lumber and wheat we produce. Not more than half of it can be sold in Canada, and when we look to use our nearest and best markets we aie up against a wall of high tariff.
Here is a man who admits that he had always been an advocate of a high protective tariff but, as he says himself now, times have changed. Well, Mr. Speaker, in concluding I might quote that old saying, that a wise man sometimes changes his mind; and much as I dislike saying unpleasant things, I cannot but add the rest of it-a fool never does.

I had not intended trespassing on the time of the House or taking part in the debate, and I would not at this
late hour venture to detain the proceedings were it not for the peculiar performance which the House has witnessed this evening on the part of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter). After having during the past months advertised himself throughout the country as the great champion of the rights of the Maritime provinces, after spending almost three months of the present session in parliament, the hon. gentleman has taken this opportunity of putting forward in his own peculiar way what he considers to be the claim of the Maritime provinces; and he has done so at midnight at the end of this protracted debate. At no time since the session opened did this wonderful champion of our rights in the Maritime provinces venture to call the attention of the House or of the country to our needs and our necessities until the present moment, and under these peculiar circumstances. The hon. gentleman has put forward remarkable claims, and made loud assertions as to the necessity for unity among all of us who come from the Maritime provinces. I may be permitted, I think, to say that hon. gentlemen who come from that part of the country view with a great deal of suspicion these high-sounding statements on the part of the hon. member. calling upon my hon. friend to resign is a fact which I think I can mention. Mr. MACDONALD (Pictou) My hon. friend says it is not correct. I am not going into the findings of the commissioner. All I say is that in view of the fact that this is on record as part of the proceedings of the legislature of New Brunswick, it is about time that my hon. friend from St. John should cease lecturing hon. gentlemen in this House with an air of serene superiority and intense holiness, an air which he has adopted ever since he came to this House. I submit that this conduct sits very badly upon a gentleman, the legislature of whose native province passed the resolution which I have referred to, which is on the records of that body, and which will remain there forever.

Mr. Speaker, I quite realize that the hour is late, and in view of the fact that the budget has been so thoroughly debated I shall not take up any more time than I can possibly help in the few remarks I am about to offer.
In so far as the tariff reductions and the provisions dealing with the sales tax are concerned, I approve of the budget. But I would call the attention of the House and of the government to the fact that there are many other items in the tariff schedules that could very well have been reduced with great benefit to the consumers of this country. In view of the high cost of living I think the government might have gone a good deal further and made such reductions as would have increased the, purchasing power of the people.
We have heard a good deal about the benefits of protection, but in my opinion there is no possibility of a protective tariff making for prosperity in this country. We must all realize this important fact, that the only way whereby wealth can be produced is
4 a.m. by applying the machinery of production and labour to the development of our natural resources, and anything that stands in the way of such development will naturally reduce the amount of real wealth that otherwise would eventually be produced.
The Budget-Mr. Gardiner

suggestion to the House, but I trust the government will take some action in regard to it this year because it is important that we should have the question of rural credits settled at the very earliest opportunity. I would remind the House also of this very important fact:	We are spending something
like $3,000,000 a year to bring settlers to this country, and what are we going to do with them when we get them here? We have no method of financing those settlers if we desire to put them upon the land. Until we have some such system it is worse than useless to spend two, three, or four million dollars a year to bring in fresh settlers to settle upon the land, and our immigration policy is absolutely ridiculous.
There is another matter I should like to refer to for a moment and that is the port of Vancouver. Representing as I do an Alberta constituency the development of the port of Vancouver is a very important necessity to us. It is estimated that we will ship through the port of Vancouver this year something like 50,000,000 bushels of grain, and as time goes on the amount of grain passing through that port will become much larger. There will also be shipped through the port of Vancouver other commodities than grain, and therefore the development of that port is a matter of great concern to us at the present time. I understand that the Board of Harbour Commissioners have made requests to the government for sums of money for different development purposes. It was rumoured at one time tfcat the amount was something like $18,000,000. Lately I have heard that the amount they are demanding is in the neighbourhood of $12,000,000. I do not know whether that is correct or not, but the government will doubtless bring down an estimate for a substantial vote of money for the development of the port of Vancouver. The reason I bring this question up to-night is this: While we would desire to see the port of Vancouver have all the facilities that are necessary for the proper carrying on of business at the present time, we are very anxious that there shall be^ no over-development at that particular point for the reason that if there is overdevelopment at that port we are satisfied the grain passing through it will have to carry the big share of the burden.
I would refer hon. members to the report of the Montreal Harbour Board, and if they look up the financial statement of that board they will find that the grain passing through the port of Montreal is bearing the big bulk of the cost of that particular port, and I submit that the charges on grain are far too

high in comparison with the service they are rendering. The same thing might become prevalent in the port of Vancouver. We as grain farmers are quite willing to pay our fair share of the charges of the port, but we are not willing to pay more than our fair share, and if there is an over-development at the port then we are satisfied that we will have to pay more than our fair share on the grain passing through that port. Another matter I would like to ask the government to take an interest in is with reference to the elevators at Vancouver. I submit with all seriousness that those elevators should be placed under the grain commission. We are not satisfied the elevators at the port of Vancouver should be wholly under the control of the harbour board. We believe the Board of Grain Commissioners is the proper authority to control these particular elevators, and I trust the government will take some action in the near future to see that these grain elevators are placed under the grain commission, and that the grain commission will have full authority over them, so far as their power goes. I would like the government to look into the matter of the port and the elevators at the port of Vancouver to see that the elevators are licensed under the Board of Grain Commissioners. If they are so licensed, then we have some control over them, but if they are not so licensed under that board, then we have practically to all intents and purposes very little control over their activities.
During the last session of this parliament a considerable sum of money was voted for an addition to the No. 1 elevator at Vancouver, and I trust the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), or the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King), whichever is the responsible official, will take cognizance of what I have to say on this particular matter. From a return we have received in this House we find that it has cost for that new construction on No. 1 elevator, 98 cents a bushel to build that elevator. In so far as the cost at the head of the lakes is concerned1, it costs usually about 23 cents a bushel to provide storage capacity. Now when we find that at the port of Vancouver it costs 98 cents instead of about 23 cents, I think we are justified in asking the government why it is that there is such an excessive cost at the port of Vancouver, as compared with the cost at the head of the lakes. Possibly the government may say that it was necessary to push on this work and make haste; but even conceding' that it was necessary to make haste, I submit that the cost is far too high. I find also

The Budget- .Ar. Gardiner
from returns made to this House that there there were no tenders let for this particular additional work to this elevator. The Pacific Construction Company did the work on a cost plus basis. It is all right to have work done on a cost plus basis, provided the cost is within reason, but when you have work done on a cost plus basis where the actual amount of money spent is perhaps three times more than it should be, then we can begin to realize that the profit, even on a cost plus basis, to the construction company is far too excessive.
Another matter I would like to bring before the House is in relation to the port of Vancouver. You will have noticed in the press some months ago where some arrangement has been made with the harbour board to buy what was known as the Woodward elevator. I understand that the foundation had only been built for this elevator when Mr. Woodward died, and we find that the Board of Harbour Commissioners has bought this foundation, bought the property in fact; but what are they going to do with it? They are going to complete it at a probable cost of $650,000, and license it to a private company, and for what purpose? For the purpose of buying grain and possibly mixing it. Now, Mr. Speaker, we know something of what is taking place in private terminal elevators or mixing houses at the head of the lakes, and I am very sorry indeed that the harbour board has allowed a mixing elevator to operate at the port of Vancouver. We must remember that this mixing elevator is going to be paid for by public funds or public credit, and I submit that it is no function of the harbour board to buy elevators and turn them over to private interests, for the exploitation of these private interests. I am going to bring to the attention of the House information furnished by the Board of Grain Commissioners to the special committee on agricultural conditions at the last session of parliament. This deals with the private terminal elevator companies or mixing houses at the head of the lakes, and I am going to give the House one example of what is happening there, so that the House and the government will realize why it is we object to the mixing houses being operated at Vancouver. On this side of the page are the different grades that go into the elevator. In this particular case there were 48 different grades that went into the elevator. In these other columns are the number of bushels of the different grades. One column represents the total number of 140
bushels of the different grades that go into this elevator. Over on the other side at the far comer appear the different grades that were shipped out. As I stated a minute ago 48 different grades went into this elevator, but only five grades came out. The grades on this side run from No. 1 northern to tough feed. We have rejected-tough and no grade running down to rejected feed, which is a pretty poor sample of wheat.
I am giving the House an opportunity to realize the different classes of grain that went into the elevator. The grades shipped out were Nos. 1, 2 and 3, No. 4 dried and No. 4 heated. That this budget has succeeded in extending the most clear cut and practical recognition of the needs of those immense new agricultural and commercial interests which have arisen in western Canada.
